The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
papers.abstract: We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

papers.title: Unintended Regulatory Spillovers: The Impact of Bank Regulatory Oversight on Environmental Enforcement
papers.abstract: We explore whether bank regulatory oversight affects the ability of environmental enforcement to reduce industrial emissions. A major objective of environmental enforcement is to reduce industrial emissions by encouraging firms to employ greener production processes and technologies. However, such changes often require external financing obtained from banks, and prior research shows that regulatory oversight of banks can affect bank lending. We find that, on average, the reduction in air pollution in response to county‐level environmental enforcement is attenuated in counties exposed to increased bank regulatory oversight, as measured by severe enforcement actions. Furthermore, we show that the negative impact of bank regulatory oversight on small business lending to affected counties is the likely mechanism behind this on‐average effect. However, when bank regulatory oversight targets banks with stronger capitalization, we find that the negative effect of bank regulatory oversight on environmental enforcement is mitigated. Collectively, our findings suggest that bank regulation has a nuanced effect on the extent to which environmental enforcement reduces emissions, indicating that one regulator's mission can impact the objectives of another.

papers.title: The effect of the mandatory disclosure of corporate tax returns on reporting bias
papers.abstract: How do investor reactions to the mandatory disclosure of firm tax information influence managers' reporting choices? To answer this question, we build a structural model of reporting bias, which we test with a unique data set of Turkish firms that have been mandated to publicly disclose their tax returns since 2009. We find that both book and tax income numbers are informative to investors. Structural estimates are consistent with disclosure of the tax report reducing both market incentives to manage book earnings and investor uncertainty about underlying firm value. Tax disclosure is associated with higher reported tax income, though the increase is not statistically significant. Counterfactual estimates suggest that book‐tax‐conformity could change financial and tax reporting biases, but lead to a lower quality information environment relative to the separate disclosure of book and tax reports.

papers.title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
papers.abstract: Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

papers.title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
papers.abstract: Although extensive research examines the costs and benefits of adopting new disclosure regulations, little addresses the consequences of regulatory inaction. We investigate whether firms in nonadopting countries incur additional information losses, beyond the forgone benefits, when their foreign peers adopt International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Nonadopters bear an absolute liquidity cost as foreign peers adopt IFRS, consistent with negative externalities from IFRS and accompanying reforms. Exploiting heterogeneity across nonadopting countries, we observe more pronounced liquidity declines among firms with greater institutional ownership overlap with IFRS peers. This effect appears more pronounced when IFRS peers are domiciled in countries with concurrent enforcement reforms or greater comparability improvements. Further evidence shows shared intermediaries—investors and analysts—reduce information production for nonadopters as other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Overall, regulatory inaction degrades information environments: resources shift to the new regime, worsening liquidity for firms in the old regime. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from commercial sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G1; K22; M41; M48.

papers.title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
papers.abstract: We investigate how generalized trust, a culturally rooted belief in the trustworthiness of unfamiliar others, influences board oversight. Using an ancestry-based measure of board–CEO trust based on ancestral origins and bilateral trust scores across countries, we find a significant positive relation between board–CEO trust and stock price crash risk, indicating higher bad-news hoarding. This relation remains robust across alternative crash risk measures, sample specifications, and trust measures. Firms with high board–CEO trust exhibit more asymmetric stock market reactions to good news versus bad news and a higher likelihood of material restatements. Analyses of insider trading patterns show that directors in high-trust firms are less informed than CEOs about adverse developments, supporting lax board monitoring rather than collusion between directors and CEOs. Overall, the evidence suggests that culturally inherited trust can weaken board oversight and reduce corporate transparency, consistent with an underexplored governance friction even within well-structured boards. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the study. JEL Classifications: G14; G34; G41; M12.

papers.title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
papers.abstract: Audit teams may consult with their firm’s national office to obtain specialized expertise, satisfy regulatory and quality control requirements, and demonstrate due professional care. We describe the consultation process based on PCAOB standards, firm methodologies, and auditor interviews. We explain different types of consultations and highlight differences in the determinants and usefulness of mandatory versus voluntary consultations. Using PCAOB inspection data, we show that formal consultations are largely predictable based on engagement characteristics and, on average, are not associated with audit quality. However, two subsets of formal consultations that focus on accounting issues and occur earlier in the engagement process are associated with greater regulatory compliance and higher audit quality. Hence, an increasing reliance on all types of consultations does not automatically translate into higher audit quality. Collectively, our findings deepen our understanding of auditors’ use of national office consultations and their implications for audit practice. Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources. JEL Classification: M4.

papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Environmental Commitments and Gas Flaring in the African Oil Sector
papers.abstract: Corporations make substantial progress toward their Zero Routine Flaring commitments globally, particularly in Africa where preexisting environmental standards are weak. Moreover, committers’ flaring reductions on the continent are driven primarily by operational improvements rather than offloading assets and are concentrated among committers facing greater stakeholder pressure. Although flaring is higher for assets continuously operated by, awarded to, or divested to noncommitters, corporate actions to uphold commitments are associated with a conservatively estimated 10 percent net reduction in flaring in Africa without a corresponding reduction in oil production or local economic activity in extraction communities. Our findings suggest that environmental commitments are backed by corporate policies akin to establishing a uniform cost of pollution across the firm’s global operations and therefore may alleviate the problems posed by globally fragmented regulation. Data Availability: All data except for Enverus oil and gas are publicly available. Enverus is available for purchase on a subscription basis. JEL Classifications: F18; K23; K32; L71; M14; M48; N57; O13; Q35; Q52; Q53; Q56.

papers.title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
papers.abstract: Mortgage fraud was a leading force behind the 2008 financial crisis. We measure the fraudulent income overstatement at the bank-ZIP Code-year level as the difference in the local growth between reported income in mortgage applications and the income based on IRS data. We find that overstated income is positively associated with banks’ internal control weaknesses over financial reporting and negatively associated with subsequent remediation of such weaknesses. The associations are concentrated among banks that integrate their accounting and operation processes, as proxied by the adoption of an Enterprise Resource Planning system. Finally, using the removal of internal control provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act in 2005 as a shock to internal control quality, we find that affected banks experience increased income overstatement on mortgage applications. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from the public and proprietary sources identified in the article. Access to proprietary data is subject to the relevant providers’ licensing restrictions. JEL Classifications: G01; G21; G28; G51; M41.

papers.title: How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
papers.abstract: This study examines how tenured BAF experience and navigate institutional structures while advancing their careers. Leveraging a qualitative approach, we find BAF encounter recurring forms of marginalization embedded in organizational structures that lead to social identity threats that destabilize their identities as scholars and teachers. BAF respond to these threats by employing agentic and self-preserving coping responses designed to affirm identity and negotiate career advancement. Although coping responses can be effective on an individual level, they do not transform institutional structures and can provoke pushback that reinscribes marginalization. The findings unsettle common assumptions that effort in conditions marked by objectivity and neutrality drives career advancement and highlight the institutional structures and invisible labor that BAF navigate to achieve career advancement. We fill the void in the literature examining how career advancement unfolds within racialized conditions of academic institutions and advance research on minoritized group status in accounting academia.

papers.title: Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
papers.abstract: Firms typically design incentive systems to motivate employees and advance firm objectives, including productivity (i.e., maximizing output) and efficiency (i.e., minimizing input). However, there remains little empirical research on the potential psychological effects of adopting a productivity versus efficiency focus on employee risk perceptions and decision-making. To address this important gap, we examine how these different incentive foci affect employee target setting under participative budgets. We predict and find that employees perceive efficiency incentives as riskier than productivity incentives, leading to lower target setting. Moreover, consistent with our theory, this effect disappears in the absence of outcome uncertainty. We also find employees are less likely to achieve their target and have higher error rates under efficiency incentives, despite setting easier targets. Overall, our findings suggest that efficiency incentives, relative to productivity incentives, can have detrimental effects on target setting and subsequent performance in participative budgeting settings. Data Availability: Contact the authors. JEL Classifications: M41; M52; J33.

papers.title: Does Free Speech Law Contribute to Corporate Social Responsibility Behavior? Empirical Evidence
papers.abstract: People’s right to free speech can have profound effects on how firms discharge their social and environmental responsibilities. We examine these effects by analyzing the impact of the staggered enactment of anti-SLAPP free speech laws across U.S. states on firms’ corporate social responsibility (CSR) behavior. We theorize that, following the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, firms enhance their CSR activities as an economically effective means to counter negative publicity from stakeholders. Supporting this idea, we find that firm CSR activity increases after the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, accompanied by an increase in stakeholder criticism of firms’ social and environmental practices. Further, we observe an increase in the level of CSR disclosure. The link between anti-SLAPP law enactment and subsequent CSR engagement is stronger in states with more comprehensive anti-SLAPP protections than in those with weaker protections. Data Availability: From public sources identified in the study. Some may require a subscription. JEL Classifications: A13; D80; K15; K22; L21; M14; O32.

papers.title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
papers.abstract: Using analyst-lender affiliation in syndicated loans as a proxy for differential access to private information, we examine how unaffiliated analysts respond to this disadvantage. We find that unaffiliated analysts are more likely to herd toward affiliated analysts following loan origination, leading to improved forecast accuracy but weaker market reactions, consistent with reduced information content. In addition, herding analysts improve their forecast accuracy for other firms in their portfolios relative to nonherding analysts, suggesting a reallocation of effort. To capture information acquisition directly, we analyze IP address data from SEC EDGAR log files and find that unaffiliated analysts increase search activity, driven primarily by those not designated as herding. Although herding behavior wanes after the first year post-loan, elevated EDGAR searches persist for three years. Overall, our study provides novel evidence on how selective access to private information influences analysts’ competitive behavior. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the text, subject to the terms and conditions of those sources. JEL Classifications: G24; G14; G29.

papers.title: IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
papers.abstract: Does going public affect the amount and type of corporate international tax planning? Using a panel of U.S. corporate tax return data from 2004 to 2018, we show that IPO completion is associated with the rapid implementation of multinational foreign tax structures. Specifically, within three years after filing for an IPO, firms (1) expand their presence in low-tax jurisdictions, (2) enter into cross-border agreements that accompany intangible asset transfers to foreign subsidiaries, and (3) increase the likelihood and level of foreign related-party income-shifting payments. Effects are strongest among firms with strong capital market pressure to hit post-IPO earnings targets, firms with high R&D spending pre-IPO, and firms with limited ability to use net operating loss carryforwards. We contribute to the nascent literature studying tax implications of IPOs by documenting the types and timing of specific tax strategies that enable public firms to remain lightly taxed in the post-IPO period. JEL Classifications: F23; H25; H26.

papers.title: Capital Market Pressure and Racial Inequality in Labor Violations
papers.abstract: Managers can boost reported earnings to meet capital market expectations by pursuing aggressive cost-minimization strategies that violate labor laws, such as pressuring frontline employees to forgo safety protocols or work off the clock. We investigate whether labor law violations, which benefit the firm at the expense of employees, fall disproportionately on nonwhite frontline employees. Across similar locations (e.g., stores or plants) within the same firm, we predict and find that locations with a higher share of nonwhite frontline employees are more likely to experience a labor law violation. This racial inequality in labor violations is especially pronounced in settings more prone to racial discrimination and during periods of acute capital market pressure to meet earnings benchmarks, providing insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed disparity. Our evidence suggests that capital market pressure is associated not only with labor violations but also with racial inequality in exposure to those violations. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text.

papers.title: Enabling Employee Adaptability to Change: The Joint Effect of Compensation Contract and Process Accountability
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate in uncertain environments, requiring employees to revise task strategies to remain effective. We examine how pay for performance (PFP) influences adaptive performance following unanticipated change and argue that process accountability moderates this effect. Although PFP increases effort, it hinders adaptation by reinforcing persistence with an existing task strategy. Process accountability channels PFP-induced motivation into deeper strategic deliberation, enabling adaptation. We test our predictions in an experiment manipulating compensation (PFP versus flat wage) and process accountability (absent, reflection-only, and present), with participants in the reflection-only condition privately reflecting on their decision-making to isolate the social-evaluative component. Results show that PFP, relative to a flat wage, decreases adaptive performance when process accountability is absent, has no significant effect under reflection-only, and increases it when process accountability is present. Additional analyses suggest that strategic deliberation partially explains this effect. The findings underscore pairing PFP with process accountability to foster adaptation. Data Availability: Data are available upon request. JEL Classifications: D91; M21; M41; M52.

papers.title: The Signaling Role of Seemingly Myopic Investment Behavior
papers.abstract: This paper analytically and empirically investigates managerial investment responses to negative shocks in firm value. In the model, managers are privately informed about the shocks’ persistence, and those facing transitory shocks strategically underinvest to boost earnings and signal financial strength to investors. The model also predicts counter-signaling: firms with strong fundamentals do not need to cut investment to convey strength. We exploit the 2003 mutual fund trading scandal as a plausibly exogenous source of price pressure. Consistent with signaling, we find that firms with greater tainted-fund ownership are more likely to meet or narrowly beat analyst forecasts by cutting R&D, and that this behavior is associated with more favorable earnings announcement returns and better long-run performance. Consistent with counter-signaling, these firms are less likely to cut R&D when they beat analyst forecasts by a wide margin. Cross-sectional tests also support the model’s comparative statics. Data Availability: All data used in the study are publicly available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: C73; D82; G23; G31; G34.

papers.title: Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
papers.abstract: I explore the nature of analysts’ climate-related discussion in their reports. Focusing on industries most exposed to climate change, I find very few reports (less than 2 percent) and a minority of analysts (less than 11 percent) discuss climate-related topics. Analysts concentrate climate-related discussion among utilities, mostly discussing renewable energy and regulatory issues. These discussions exhibit no significant association with short-term earnings forecasts and a weak association with more pessimistic long-term growth forecast revisions. Climate-related discussion is also associated with more optimistic target prices when analysts do not issue long-term growth forecasts, suggesting the development of a long-term perspective correlates with views on climate-related issues. Discussions of solar-, emissions-, and automotive-related topics are associated with this greater target price optimism. These findings highlight how analysts’ climate-related discussion relates to long-term expectations and concentrates among highly exposed firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. A detailed listing of how each large language model (LLM) classified each climate-related report, a document describing the details of this listing, a firm-year summary of climate-related discussion and subtopical classifications, and a description document of this firm-year summary are available upon request. JEL Classifications: Q56; G24; M41.

papers.title: Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
papers.abstract: We examine whether audit partners’ ownership stakes in affiliated non-audit businesses are related to audit quality. We argue that non-audit ownership is a relatively sharp measure of auditor-client economic bonding, which can impair auditor independence. Using a unique setting in China where we observe partners’ equity stakes in both audit and non-audit businesses, we find that audit adjustments are significantly smaller when engagement partners hold larger ownership stakes in non-audit businesses. Audit adjustments are further reduced when the entire audit partnership holds greater ownership in affiliated non-audit businesses, suggesting that non-audit ownership matters at the audit firm level as well. Additional analyses suggest that these results are driven by impaired independence, rather than partner distraction or endogenous partner-client matching. Our study informs ongoing policy debates on the structuring of audit and non-audit businesses as well as the investments of non-audit entities in accounting practices. Data Availability: The authors have nondisclosure and confidentiality agreements for their use of proprietary data, which were provided to the authors for independent academic research only. Nonproprietary data are available from sources identified in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48; M52.

papers.title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain
papers.abstract: I examine how the use of sales performance measures in CEO incentive contracts affects the operations of a firm and its suppliers. A growing number of firms are evaluating and compensating their CEOs based on sales performance. However, because sales performance measures are narrow measures that do not incentivize cost control, they can influence operational decisions that affect not only the firm but also its suppliers. I show that the use of sales performance measures in CEO bonus contracts is associated with inventory fluctuations that increase the bullwhip effect, a phenomenon in which a firm exhibits greater volatility in production than in demand, thereby increasing the order volatility faced by its suppliers. Instrumental variable tests using the firm’s network connections through compensation consultants mitigate concerns that the results are driven by omitted factors. Collectively, my findings illuminate spillover effects of CEO incentive contracts on economically linked firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M10; M12; M40; M41; M52.

papers.title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
papers.abstract: Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

papers.title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
papers.abstract: Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

papers.title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
papers.abstract: Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

papers.title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
papers.abstract: We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

papers.title: Measurement Error, Manipulation, and the Value of Short‐Term Performance in Job Retention
papers.abstract: This paper studies how the accuracy of a short‐term performance measure affects its value when a principal decides whether to retain or fire an agent, who can manipulate that measure. Compared with ignoring performance and never firing the agent, the performance measure is valuable when the savings in the expected cost of the retention error is more than the expected cost of the firing error. A more accurate performance measure can have a non‐monotonic effect on its value: Greater accuracy improves the principal's ability to correctly identify the agent, which increases efficient firing, but it causes the incompetent agent to increase manipulation to avoid being fired, which increases inefficient retention. With a less accurate performance measure, the incompetent agent has weaker incentives for manipulation, and an increase in accuracy increases its value due to the identification effect. With a more accurate performance measure, the manipulation effect dominates, and an increase in accuracy decreases its value. The results imply that the principal prefers an imperfect performance measure when the agent can choose the level of manipulation.

papers.title: Auditors' Response to Clients' Cyber Breaches: A Human‐Capital Perspective
papers.abstract: Using online job postings data, we explore whether auditors adjust their human capital in response to clients' cyber breach incidents. We find that audit offices increase their demand for cybersecurity specialists after their clients' cyber breaches, implying that cyber breaches change not only client risk but also their auditor's production function. Consistent with expectations, we document that this impact is larger when breaches involve their own clients (rather than those of peer offices within the same audit firm) and when breaches directly involve financial information. Our evidence holds for both cyber‐focused and non‐cyber‐focused offices, highlighting the broad impact of cybersecurity risks on audit practices. Additionally, we find that audit offices with relatively high investment in cybersecurity human capital are better able to preserve their market share among clients in high‐cyber‐risk industries after a client's cyber breach.

papers.title: Would a Balanced PCAOB Inspection Approach Increase Auditors' Use of Innovative Audit Procedures?
papers.abstract: Prior research criticizes PCAOB inspection reports for focusing solely on audit deficiencies, arguing that this encourages auditors to pursue traditional procedures to demonstrate compliance with standards rather than procedures that maximize audit quality. We contribute to this debate by examining whether the PCAOB's approach discourages auditors from considering innovative audit procedures (that are potentially more effective), since they are, by definition, less standard. We compare the PCAOB's current inspection approach (which focuses on reporting audit deficiencies) to a balanced inspection approach that discloses examples of audit strengths as well as deficiencies discovered during inspections. We predict and find that when the risk of material misstatement (RMM) is moderate, a balanced inspection approach leads auditors to consider the potential effectiveness of innovative audit procedures to a greater extent, ultimately prioritizing more of them in audit plans. Our findings contribute to both research and practice by enhancing our understanding of ways to encourage audit innovation and ultimately improve overall audit quality.

papers.title: Could That Happen to Me? Auditor Response When Colleagues Are Named in Lawsuits
papers.abstract: Litigation risk is an important source of motivation for auditors to conduct high‐quality audits, but theory suggests that certain lawsuits will have a more salient disciplining effect on auditor behavior. To this end, we identify lawsuits naming an individual partner as a co‐defendant along with the audit firm. We then examine how these lawsuits affect subsequent behavior of other auditors in the office of the sued partner. Relative to lawsuits naming only the firm, our results indicate that lawsuits naming individual partners as co‐defendants are significant office‐level events that motivate a meaningful response from non‐sued audit partners in the form of higher quality and fees on existing clients and more careful client portfolio management. These results have practical implications about how auditor litigation incentivizes individual auditors to fulfill their professional duties. For regulators and audit firms seeking to promote audit quality, these findings highlight the disciplining effect of auditors' concern for their personal reputation and litigation exposure. Furthermore, audit committees, clients, and investors may observe elevated audit quality, effort, and fees following partner‐level litigation in the local office.

papers.title: Accounting and the fragmented self: institutional opacity, spiritual inequality and moral burden in Islamic finance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how Islamic financial institutions, despite claiming ethical legitimacy, may reproduce spiritual and moral inequalities. Drawing on Muhammad Iqbal's concept of khudi (Self), the study examines how institutional opacity, limited theological engagement and compliance-oriented practices displace moral responsibility onto individuals, forcing consumers to navigate financial choices amid guilt, uncertainty and fragmented ethical agency. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a qualitative interpretive approach, drawing on 30 semi-structured interviews with UK-based Muslim consumers who currently hold or have previously held Islamic financial products. The data were analysed thematically to explore how individuals experience ethical ambiguity, self-surveillance and clerical authority, and how they resist the commodification of their faith within modern financial systems. Findings Rather than a transparent ethical alternative, Islamic finance asserts moral authority without substantive justification. Facing institutional opacity and limited theological reasoning, participants internalise moral risk through guilt and self-surveillance. This uneven clarity erodes trust in religious authority, intensifies spiritual disorientation, and exposes how institutions can privatise accountability while retaining institutional legitimacy. Research limitations/implications By introducing khudi as a counter-accountability framework to demonstrate that inequalities take spiritual and moral forms, the study offers a new ontological lens for reimagining accountability as a dialogical and emancipatory practice. It urges institutions, Shariah boards and standard-setters to move beyond formal, audit-driven compliance. It repositions accountability as a substantive ethical practice, demanding that claims of Islamic legitimacy be structurally transparent and publicly justified. Originality/value Extending critical accounting scholarship, the study reveals that inequality in Islamic finance is spiritual and moral. By introducing Iqbal's khudi (Self), it provides a novel framework demonstrating how calculative regimes can either fragment or sustain the transcendent Self, repositioning accountability as a site for reclaiming spiritual agency.

papers.title: Binding the present and orchestrating the future: accounting as a technology of government in water sustainability
papers.abstract: Purpose The paper explains how water sustainability becomes governable in fragmented hybrid settings. It shows how accounting and accountability hold together diverse actors, competing obligations and different rationalities, enabling sustainability aspirations to translate into coordinated action. The paper illuminates the fragile character of this process, showing how accounting and accountability partially stabilise tensions without resolving them. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts an interpretive case study of an Italian water utility undergoing regulatory and organisational changes. It applies Dean's analytics of government framework to analyse data from interviews, sustainability reports and publicly available documents. Findings The study identifies four regimes of practice through which water sustainability was rendered governable. Across these regimes, accounting and accountability perform “binding” and “orchestrating” roles in governing water sustainability. These practices establish norms, responsibilities and incentives (binding) and align actors and activities (orchestrating), thereby stabilising but not resolving inter-regime tensions. Practical implications The study helps multiple actors, such as managers, policymakers and stakeholders, to understand how accounting and accountability can support the organisation of collective responsibility for water sustainability. Social implications The study shows how accounting and accountability redistribute responsibility for water sustainability across organisations and communities in hybrid public–private settings. In doing so, they can promote collective responsibility for water conservation but may also normalise particular ways of valuing water. Originality/value The paper introduces the concepts of binding and orchestrating to explain how accounting and accountability render sustainability governable in fragmented hybrid settings. Its value lies in showing how accounting enables collective action while leaving unresolved tensions among economic, public-service and environmental commitments visible.

papers.title: Cisnormative accounting organizations: recording the experiences of transgender people in Brazil
authors: Silvia Pereira de Castro Casa Nova
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to record, understand and problematize, in the light of transfeminism, the experiences of transgender people who have transited and/or are transiting through accounting organizations in Brazil. Design/methodology/approach This article provides detailed information on the oppression present in accounting offices in Brazil and how oppressive actions impact the experiences of trans workers in the workplace. Six semi-structured interviews were conducted with: a) two transgender women, b) two transgender men and c) two non-binary people, with various identity markers in relation to gender, race, sexuality, age, disability and socio-economic class. The stories were categorized and analyzed using Dialogic Thematic Analysis. After the analysis, we present a map of resistance strategies in the Brazilian accounting environment. Findings The participants reported negative experiences in organizational accounting environments in Brazil, marked by prejudice, discrimination, disrespect for gender identity, erroneous pronoun treatment and physical and psychological violence committed by cisgender managers and co-workers, mainly cisgender men. We identified the use of resistance strategies in these environments in the participants' narratives, including the development of technical skills, professional experience, remote training and the use of cisgender passability as a coping mechanism. Originality/value This study makes significant contributions to understanding the experiences of transgender workers in accounting organizations in Brazil, the most oppressive country for this population in the world. Our findings fill gaps in the literature on the experiences of non-cisgender gender identities in accounting and can help improve corporate actions for the inclusion, permanence and belonging of diverse people in accounting organizations. This study also contributes to the gap in the literature, encouraging the development of new studies so that the voices of trans workers can be heard, stories can be told and recorded and oppression denounced.

papers.title: Constructing sustainability expertise: capital conversion and the making of a sustainability CFO
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how a Chief Financial Officer (CFO) in a Sri Lankan state-owned bank constructed sustainability accounting as a new domain of professional expertise. Extending Baxter and Chua's (2008) conception of accounting expertise as an organisational accomplishment, the paper asks how entirely new forms of accounting expertise are constructed before organisational legitimacy, evaluative criteria and professional jurisdiction have been established, drawing on Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital to explain this process. Design/methodology/approach The study uses a longitudinal qualitative case study of a CFO in a Sri Lankan state-owned housing bank, whose sustainability agenda developed during the country's post-tsunami reconstruction. Data were collected across two phases (2013–2014) using 44 semi-structured interviews with 25 participants, supplemented by field notes and documentary analysis of sustainability reports, policy documents and media coverage. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, proceeding from inductive coding through temporal coding to theoretical interpretation via Baxter and Chua (2008) and Bourdieu, tracing the sequential conversion of cultural, symbolic, social and positional capital. Findings Sustainability accounting expertise was constructed through a cumulative process of capital conversion. An entrepreneurial habitus generated the disposition to recognise emerging opportunities, enabling the accumulation of cultural capital through learning, authorship and reporting innovation. This cultural capital was converted into symbolic capital through managerial endorsement and award recognition, which expanded social capital through strategic alliances, and was ultimately converted into positional authority, redefining the finance function's organisational jurisdiction. However, this expertise construction did not automatically translate into institutionalisation: sustainability expertise remained concentrated in a single individual rather than becoming embedded in organisational systems and routines. Research limitations/implications The single-case design prioritises theoretical development over statistical generalisation; future research should examine whether similar processes of expertise construction occur across different organisational, professional and national settings. The case also centres on an unusually entrepreneurial CFO, and alternative trajectories may emerge where sustainability initiatives are collectively led or externally mandated. The longitudinal design captured the construction of expertise but not its longer-term reproduction following leadership succession, pointing to a need for future research on how such expertise diffuses, evolves or declines once its original architect departs the organisation. Practical implications Organisations should not equate the success of a prominent sustainability champion with the institutionalisation of sustainability capability. Individual actors can mobilise resources, secure legitimacy and accelerate organisational innovation, but sustained transformation depends on converting individually held expertise into collective organisational capability. Building durable sustainability capacity therefore requires deliberate investment in knowledge sharing, succession planning and cross-functional learning, alongside organisational systems that embed expertise beyond the individual who originally constructed it, reducing organisations' dependence on any single actor for the continuity of their sustainability agenda. Originality/value The paper offers a distinctive contribution by reconceptualising accounting expertise as something that must first be constructed, rather than simply organisationally accomplished, in emerging domains such as sustainability accounting. By integrating Bourdieu's theory of field, habitus and capital with Baxter and Chua's (2008) framework, it identifies cumulative capital conversion as the specific social mechanism underlying this process – a mechanism not previously articulated in the sustainability accounting literature. It further offers the original insight that expertise construction and organisational institutionalisation are analytically distinct, showing that individually constructed expertise can achieve legitimacy while remaining fragile and undiffused across the organisation.

papers.title: Accounting for the working conditions of social compliance auditors investigating modern slavery in supply chains
papers.abstract: Purpose This study explores the working conditions of social compliance auditors who investigate modern slavery in global supply chains. This issue is important for understanding how auditors' working environment shapes audits as a key mechanism for detecting modern slavery. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 32 interviews with actors involved in social compliance auditing, including auditors, certification bodies, NGOs and accreditation agencies. Drawing on labour process theory and the complex role of multi-principal employment networks, we analyse how the work of auditing, the objects of that work and the instruments that structure it organises control, dependency and risk across external modern slavery audits. Findings Our findings show that social compliance auditing can be intensive, under-resourced work in remote, often hostile settings, producing heightened vulnerability for auditors. We also find that auditors periodically face physical harm and managerial coercion, including intimidation, violence and efforts to manipulate or suppress critical findings precisely because those findings pose a threat to business interests when non-compliant labour practices are found. Nonetheless, we show how auditors draw on “buffers of culpability” which include micro-resistance, safety-driven adaptation and agentic use of informal tools, relationships and planning, to preserve some investigative integrity despite these adverse conditions. Originality/value Businesses are increasingly held accountable for labour conditions in their supply chains and rely on social compliance auditors to independently assess operating facilities, yet auditors' own working conditions and structural vulnerabilities remain poorly understood. We specify implications at both agentic (micro) and structural (macro) levels for the governance and reform of social compliance auditing in the context of fragmented and multi-principal employment networks.

papers.title: The great slowdown? Trajectories of sustainability reporting boundary change from a value chain perspective 1990–2020
papers.abstract: Purpose As sustainability has become an increasingly urgent and critical challenge, firms have faced growing expectations to broaden the scope of accountability by extending their sustainability reporting boundaries. This article analyses sustainability boundary change from a value chain perspective across different phases of sustainability reporting. Design/methodology/approach We analysed sustainability boundaries, i.e. the extent to which a firm accounts for impacts across its own operations and wider value chain, in a single value chain of steel-adjacent firms in Sweden, using a firm- and value chain-level assessment framework developed in the article. Reports from 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020 were analysed qualitatively and quantitatively to identify boundary trajectories based on an institutional theory framing. Findings Boundaries expanded significantly between 1990 and 2020; however, this trajectory slowed between 2010 and 2020 as sustainability reporting became stabilised as a practice, with extensions primarily occurring upstream rather than downstream or societally. No firms were found to use holistic reporting by including a full value chain perspective. Research limitations/implications Firm-centric reporting is shown to be the dominant approach over time; this sits in tension with mounting expectations to report on sustainability topics more broadly. It is suggested that future studies explore other institutional contexts, countries and value chain configurations to support and expand on the findings. Studies on a more granular level than the 10-year increments used in this study could also reveal nuances of boundary extension over time. Originality/value We distinguish between scope and depth, two dimensions of sustainability boundaries, to develop a framework of boundary approaches: firm-limited reporting, insular reporting, value chain aware reporting and holistic reporting. Based on these, we identify opportunities and challenges for adopting a value chain perspective in sustainability reporting, noting that, while the number of topics (i.e. depth) can be increased by using reporting frameworks like Global Reporting Initiative, incorporating topics at the value chain level (i.e. scope) remains a key challenge for firms due to the firm-centric logic used in both financial and sustainability reporting.

papers.title: Cultural intermediation through indigenous values-based accountability: the case of Bangarra Dance Theatre
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how Indigenous values shape the accountability practices governing cultural intermediation. It investigates how accountability enables Indigenous relational governance to be sustained as Indigenous cultural knowledge circulates through cultural intermediation while remaining aligned with Indigenous custodial authority. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on a qualitative, longitudinal case study of Bangarra Dance Theatre, an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisation operating as a cultural intermediary in Australia. Data were collected over twelve years through a combination of participant observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentary materials. Findings The analysis identifies Indigenous Values-Based Accountability as a set of interconnected accountability practices through which Indigenous relational governance is sustained. Through permission seeking, cultural observation, creative obligation, and return and renewal, IVBA organises Bangarra's continuing accountability as Indigenous cultural knowledge circulates across public and cross-cultural domains while sustaining Indigenous custodial authority. The findings further demonstrate how IVBA structures participation in cultural circulation by making engagement by sponsors, partners, and other external actors conditional upon Indigenous custodial authority. Originality/value This paper advances Indigenous accounting and accountability research by conceptualising accountability as a culturally embedded governance arrangement through which Indigenous values are enacted beyond Indigenous organisational and community settings. It demonstrates how Indigenous relational governance organises authority, reciprocity, and custodial responsibility as cultural knowledge circulates across public and cross-cultural domains. The paper further positions cultural intermediation as a distinctive accountability setting that, in our case, involves Bangarra remaining accountable to recognised custodians while Indigenous authority structures participation, representation, and engagement with non-Indigenous actors.

papers.title: Sustainability accounting and reporting: organisational identity construction and enactment in local governments
papers.abstract: Purpose Sustainability accounting and reporting (SAR) has experienced a wide diffusion in the last decades, also in the public sector. It is primarily useful for increasing accountability, transparency and organisational legitimacy. As a consequence, scholars have focused their attention on the external dimensions of SAR and its relationship with organisations' financial performance. This focus has left the internal and managerial dimension of SAR largely underexplored. This article seeks to address this gap by shedding light on the role that SAR can play in the processes of organisational identity construction and enactment. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal case study was conducted to examine the ongoing voluntary adoption of SAR by an Italian pioneer municipality (MoB), and how this practice has contributed to its identity construction and enactment. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and official documents. Findings The research identifies voluntary SAR as both driven by organisational identity and used to construct and enact it in the absence of a public policy. More specifically, SAR contributes to organisational identity construction and enactment by building a collective memory that demonstrates the alignment and consistency between public employees' work and the identity of the organisation to which they belong. Originality/value The research advances the literature on SAR by exploring its contribution to studies on organisational identity. It analyses documents that reflect various phases of organisational processes (planning, accounting and reporting) as organisational practices that contribute to the construction and enactment of organisational identity. The absence of an explicit public policy could be seen as undermining the role of SAR as an accountability tool. Instead, this article shows that voluntary SAR may operate internally as a technology through which organisational identity is articulated, stabilised and enacted over time. This perspective highlights the organisational potential of SAR beyond its external accountability function.

papers.title: Expense disclosures and the social meaning of charitable donations
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how donors use expense disclosures when evaluating charities. Design/methodology/approach We conducted 35 interviews with individual donors using a vignette-based method, combining Zelizer's (2012, 1997) theory of the social meaning of money with Kolhede and Gomez-Arias’ (2022) donor typology of “impressionable”, “intrinsic” and “sceptic” donors. Findings Donors interpret expense disclosures through relational and moral frameworks rather than purely technical or economic ones. Impressionable donors treat expense information primarily as a trust signal, relying more on social cues and reputation. Intrinsic donors use ethical, mission-focused reasoning, valuing explanations of how spending benefits beneficiaries. Sceptic donors engage analytically, using disclosures to judge integrity, efficiency and legitimacy. Impressionable, intrinsic and sceptic donors focused not only on how much was spent, but on whether expenditure was perceived to meaningfully contribute to the charities’ mission and outcomes. Research limitations/implications Our findings suggest that donor behaviour cannot be fully understood through economic models alone and call for greater attention to the social and ethical dimensions of financial information. We also highlight the limitations of standard expense classifications and the need for more contextualised disclosures. Practical implications Charities should provide expense disclosures that are layered and inclusive, combining numerical clarity, contextual explanation and value-based narratives to address differing information needs. Doing so can help build trust, avoid the nonprofit starvation cycle, and foster stronger, more sustainable donor relationships. Originality/value We reconceptualise expense disclosures as part of relational work, showing that donors assign moral and symbolic meaning to financial data, challenging assumptions of purely rational donor behaviour.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Audit Oversight under One Roof: The Impact of Engagement Quality Reviewer Proximity
papers.abstract: Engagement quality review is a cornerstone of audit firms’ quality control systems. We examine whether same-office engagement quality reviewer (EQR) assignments are associated with audit quality and market perceptions. Using unique data on EQR identities, we find that same-office EQR assignments are generally associated with higher audit quality outcomes. These associations are significant among non-Big 4 firms and when EQRs have lower industry expertise or face higher workload constraints, whereas same-office EQR assignments are associated with lower audit quality among EQRs and engagement partners with strong within-firm network ties. Additional analyses suggest that the association between EQR proximity and audit quality is concentrated in same-office assignments and varies across levels of geographic distance. We further document negative market reactions to announcements of EQRs moving from the same office to a different office, indicating that markets price the loss of within-office EQR oversight. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; M43.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Remote Auditing and Audit Quality: Evidence from the Field
papers.abstract: We investigate the impact of remote auditing on audit quality and identify the good practices auditors adopt to improve audit quality in remote auditing. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in China provides an opportune testing ground for analyzing this issue. Using both survey and archival data, we document that audit quality, on average, declines when auditors switch to remote auditing following the outbreak of the pandemic. More importantly, this decline is not an inherent consequence of remote work: audit quality is largely maintained when auditors enhance risk evaluation and data analysis, make timely adjustments to audit procedures, emphasize the sufficiency and reliability of digital evidence, and leverage information and communication technology. Our findings can help financial statement users better understand the quality of audits conducted virtually and offer implications for practitioners to improve audit quality in remote settings. Data Availability: The archival data used in this study were obtained from the China Stock Market & Accounting Research (CSMAR) database and are available from the data provider. The survey data are not publicly available because they contain confidential information about respondents and their audit engagements. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; O33.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Client-Engaged Specialists, Estimation Risk, and Auditor Attention
papers.abstract: This study examines whether auditors adjust attention in response to reliability signals of client-engaged specialists. I exploit the Canadian oil and gas setting, where listed firms must engage and disclose independent reserve evaluators to provide assurance on reserve estimates. Measuring evaluator-revealed performance and associated estimation risk with past portfolio negative revisions, I find that a higher past negative revision rate is associated with higher audit fees, longer audit report lags, and a greater likelihood of late annual filings. The association is present for revisions at both the focal client and other companies in the evaluator’s portfolio, evident for technical and more recent revisions, and stronger when estimation uncertainty is high. Higher negative revision rates are also associated with reserve-related going concern opinions and key audit matter disclosures, but not output-based audit quality. The findings suggest that auditors incorporate specialist performance signals when assessing specialist-related estimation risk and allocating attention. Data Availability: Data obtained from CanOils Database Ltd. and Compustat are available from the respective providers under license. Hand-collected audit report, restatement, filing, and reserve disclosure information is drawn from publicly available issuer filings on SEDAR/SEDAR+. The author can provide additional information about data construction, subject to the applicable licensing and redistribution restrictions. JEL Classifications: M41; M42.

papers.journal: Auditing: A Journal of Practice and Theory
papers.title: Do Auditors Treat Clients Engaging in Research and Development Differently When Issuing Going Concern Modifications?
papers.abstract: Companies with research and development (R&D) activity operate differently from traditional companies because they depend more on innovation to generate value. Analyzing R&D companies is challenging because R&D accounting treatment reduces current earnings and does not fully capture future value. We investigate whether and how R&D expenditures impact auditor going concern modification (GCM) decisions. We document a positive relation between R&D intensity and the likelihood of a GCM. We also find a positive relation between R&D intensity and GCM accuracy in terms of the likelihood of Type II errors (i.e., bankrupt clients not receiving a GCM). Finally, we show that auditors of R&D companies put less weight on traditional accounting-based bankruptcy metrics when issuing GCMs than do auditors of non-R&D companies. We contribute to the auditing literature examining the issuances of GCMs and to research examining the evaluation of R&D company operations and performance. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G33; M4; M42.

Ancestor's Legacy? The Effect of Folklore on Corporate Innovation
papers.abstract: This paper investigates how ancestral narratives shape contemporary corporate innovation. Drawing on pre‐industrial folklore from 20 countries, we exploit within‐country variation in local cultural motifs to examine their impact on firm innovation. We focus on two types of motifs: narratives depicting heroes’ successful challenges relative to challenge‐losing ones and narratives containing supernatural entities. We show that firms located in societies whose local folklore prevalently features heroes overcoming challenges exhibit greater R&D investment and higher patent‐based innovation efficiency, with directionally similar but statistically insignificant evidence for citation‐based efficiency. In contrast, firms in societies where folklore emphasizes supernatural entities display lower R&D investment and lower innovation efficiency. Cross‐sectional analyses indicate that these effects are moderated by regional economic openness and national patent protection and are more pronounced in highly innovative industries and among firms with higher levels of corporate transparency. Our findings are robust after controlling for regional factors or alleviating large country sample bias. The relationship between folklore and R&D investment remains directionally consistent, albeit with lower statistical significance, after instrumenting the folklore measure with historical immigration patterns to the United States. We further show that the net prevalence of challenge‐encouraging motifs is associated with more radical innovation strategies and greater corporate risk‐taking, while supernatural motifs exhibit the opposite pattern. Overall, our findings support the view that folklore persists across generations and meaningfully influences firms’ contemporary economic decisions and outcomes.

papers.title: Contextualization of Numbers in Earnings Conference Calls
papers.abstract: Prior research generally finds that using numbers in financial disclosure is beneficial. However, numbers can also be strategically proffered due to their perceived precision and informativeness. We find the use of undercontextualized numbers in earnings conference calls is associated with short‐term benefits but negative longer‐term consequences. Specifically, undercontextualization is associated with a short‐term positive market return, positive analyst forecast revisions, and a more positive tone in analysts’ questions. Furthermore, we find undercontextualization is associated with a longer‐term negative market return, a decrease in year‐over‐year earnings, and a higher incidence of restatements. In additional analyses, we find evidence consistent with the intentional use of undercontextualization, as it is associated with conference call casting, insider trading, and internal information quality. Given the uniqueness of our measure, we provide evidence of its validity by documenting its association with analyst scrutiny and other proxies for strategic call behavior. Finally, we examine a mechanism underlying our results and find evidence that undercontextualized numbers have a greater influence on retail investors.

papers.title: The Effects of Promotion Patterns Within Audit Firms on Audit Adjustments: Insights Into Promotion Speed and Flexibility
papers.abstract: This study investigates how promotion patterns within audit firms impact audit adjustments. Using detailed data on partner promotions in Chinese audit firms, we measure firm‐level promotion speed and promotion flexibility and examine their effects on audit adjustments. We find that auditors in audit firms with faster and more flexible promotion patterns are more likely to make audit adjustments. Additional analyses show that firmwide promotion speed and flexibility are positively associated with the likelihood of both upward and downward adjustments, as well as the magnitude of audit adjustments. Cross‐sectional analyses indicate that the effects of promotion patterns on audit adjustments are more pronounced in larger audit firms, with the effect of promotion speed being stronger among lower ranked auditors facing greater promotion incentives. Additionally, fast and flexible promotion patterns improve audit efficiency. Organizational reform also shapes promotion patterns, as the adoption of the limited liability partnership (LLP) structure is associated with faster partner promotion. Overall, this study provides initial evidence of the effect of promotion patterns on audit outcomes.

Does Corporate Accountability Towards Biodiversity Loss and Species Extinction Protection Account for Audit Efforts: New Insights from External Auditing
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether and how corporate biodiversity disclosure affects external audit efforts. Using a deep‐learning‐expanded text analysis of corporate social responsibility reports for heavily polluting Chinese companies from 2009 to 2021, this paper examines the relation between biodiversity disclosure and audit efforts. The empirical evidence reveals that firms with more extensive biodiversity disclosure exhibit significantly greater external audit efforts. The results remain robust to a series of endogeneity checks, including two‐stage least squares estimation and a combined propensity score matching and difference‐in‐differences analysis. Further analyses show that this positive relation is more pronounced for non‐state‐owned enterprises and firms located in eastern China. Mechanism tests reveal that biodiversity disclosure by heavy polluters triggers a ‘horn effect’, which elevates auditors' perceptions of composite audit risk, thereby driving greater audit effort. Interestingly, while biodiversity disclosures increase audit duration, they do not translate into higher audit fees. Collectively, the findings demonstrate that corporate biodiversity accountability increases audit risk and effort, highlighting the economic consequences of sustainability reporting within the auditing context.

papers.title: Does the Facial Trustworthiness of Hosting Staff Lead to Forecast Bias? Evidence from Analysts’ Site Visits
papers.abstract: We use unique data about corporate site visits in China to examine whether face‐to‐face interactions introduce bias in analyst forecasts. We find that analysts tend to issue more optimistic forecasts when accompanied by hosting staff with high facial trustworthiness, indicating a cognitive bias. This effect is amplified when firms convey more positive information during visits, but is attenuated for firms with high disclosure quality, for experienced and star analysts, for analysts with science, technology, engineering, and mathematics backgrounds, and for analysts visiting industry peers concurrently. Furthermore, the bias is stronger for sole‐visiting analysts but diminishes over time as additional information becomes available or with repeated interactions. Additional analyses show that forecast accuracy also declines, but the effect of facial trustworthiness does not extend to analysts’ stock recommendations or market reactions. Overall, our findings highlight that even sophisticated analysts are susceptible to cognitive bias in face‐to‐face interactions, while alternative information sources, professional experience, and repeated engagement help mitigate such bias.
