Domain Knowledge and Human-AI Collaboration: Extracting Accounting Information from Contracts
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Contracts govern how firms invest, borrow, and recognize revenue, but their length, technical terms, and nested cross-references make large-sample extraction slow and error-prone. We examine whether generative AI (GenAI) can ease this task and what role accountants’ expertise plays. Framing the division of labor through Becker and Murphy (1992) specialization theory, we develop an iterative, human-in-the-loop prompt engineering workflow in which the model interprets contractual terms and a human verifier corrects its output. Nine variants across debt, lease, and sales contracts vary the presence of a human verification loop and the verifier’s accounting expertise. Accuracy rises with both expertise depth and verification intensity, and the two are complementary. A nonaccountant loop drops accuracy below the no-loop baseline, whereas an accountant reaches higher accuracy at lower cost and catches model failures. For firms and researchers staffing contract analysis, deep human domain knowledge is the scarce input, not only GenAI access. Data Availability: The contracts analyzed in this study are publicly available from SEC EDGAR. The prompts used in each workflow are reproduced in the Online Appendix. JEL Classifications: M41; C81; O33; J24; G32; K12.

papers.title: Trading Patterns Before Unscheduled Corporate Announcements
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Using comprehensive trade-level data from India’s National Stock Exchange, covering 1,491 unscheduled corporate announcements between 2011 and 2015, we identify which categories of traders position themselves profitably in the days before public disclosure. Retail traders, and to a lesser extent proprietary manual traders, accumulate positions in the direction of the impending announcement; institutional and algorithmic traders do not. The advantage is concentrated in good news events (consistent with short-sale constraints) and in smaller stocks and is absent before scheduled earnings announcements or randomized placebo events. The pattern is consistent with insider-origin information diffusing through informal networks—broker chatter, messaging app groups, and social media—into a noisy signal that the least constrained traders can act upon but compliance-bound institutions cannot. The findings have implications for the design of pre-announcement disclosure rules and the monitoring of informal communication channels. Data Availability: The NSE trade-level data were obtained from the National Stock Exchange of India for academic research and are subject to the Exchange’s data-sharing restrictions. Announcement and firm-level data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G14; G15; G18.

papers.title: Nonfinancial Rating Agencies, Stakeholder Pressure, and Social Externalities
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Nonfinancial rating (NFR) agencies improve the transparency of firms’ ESG practices, but their coverage remains incomplete. This study examines whether the information produced by NFR agencies generates social externalities beyond rated firms. Using staggered coverage by four major NFR agencies from 2000 to 2018, we find that uncovered firms have fewer regulatory ESG violations when a larger share of firms in the same state or industry is covered by NFR agencies. The effect is stronger where stakeholder demand for ESG information is higher and for firms with greater visibility to analysts, media, and institutional investors. Additional tests based on headquarters relocation, ESG-related news, violation categories, alternative specifications, an extended 2000–2025 sample, and state-exclusion analyses support this interpretation. Our evidence suggests that NFR agencies not only discipline rated firms but also improve stakeholders’ ability to monitor unrated firms, with implications for investors and regulators facing incomplete firm-level ESG information.

papers.title: Yuji Ijiri (1935–2017): Measurement, Accountability, and Accounting as a Social Institution
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Yuji Ijiri (1935–2017) helped define accounting as an intellectual field and a social institution. This memorial examines his scholarship and leadership through the themes of accountability and accounting structure. His accountability framework directed attention to the rights and obligations of those giving and receiving an account. We examine how his work on historical cost, momentum, and triple-entry accounting connected measurement to accountability. Drawing on published and archival sources, we connect these ideas to his work within the Graduate School of Industrial Administration (GSIA), Carnegie Mellon, the American Accounting Association, and trans-Pacific scholarly exchange. Building on earlier tributes, we trace the development and reception of his ideas alongside the institutions that sustained his inquiry. His legacy joins formal analysis, attention to accounting’s responsibilities, and stewardship of a diverse scholarly community. Data Availability: The published and archival sources supporting this article are identified in the references, footnotes, and Table 1. Archival records cited in this article are held by Carnegie Mellon University Archives. JEL Classifications: M41; B31; B32.

papers.title: Personnel Controls and Learning in Hybrid Work: The Co-Construction of Control
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Hybrid work disrupts the controls accounting firms traditionally use to ensure learning and develop professional expertise. Drawing on 42 semistructured interviews with managers and associates in Big 4 firms during the transition from remote to hybrid work, we examine how personnel controls function under these conditions. We contribute to management control research by showing that personnel controls are no longer solely firm-operated mechanisms but co-constructed by firms and associates, reshaping how they produce their intended outcomes. Further, we show that this co-construction redistributes responsibility for learning, requiring more deliberate and effortful engagement from associates. Although personnel controls continue to improve communication and clarify expectations, they become less effective in developing professional expertise, with managers and associates experiencing these outcomes differently. We conclude that personnel controls should not be assumed to simultaneously sustain performance and ensure learning, highlighting the need for employee engagement in the co-construction of control. Data Availability: The data that support the findings of this study are available upon request. The data are not publicly available since they contain information that could compromise the privacy of research participants. JEL Classifications: M12.

papers.title: Implementing IFRS 9: Evidence from Financial Institution Preparers on Expected Credit Loss Reporting
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Despite emerging research on the adoption and effects of the expected credit loss (ECL) approach introduced by IFRS 9, its operational realities remain largely unexamined. Drawing on evidence from semistructured interviews with senior financial reporting and risk professionals, we examine how preparers implement the approach. We find that preparers design ECL models that are closely aligned with their internal risk management. A forward-looking approach is operationalized through the development of a range of probability-weighted future scenarios. ECL models are highly customized, and one of the key challenges is the need for continuous monitoring. Overall, we find that preparers appreciate the flexibility provided by the ECL approach but also recognize that its implementation entails managerial judgment variability and introduces potential model risk. Our findings should interest auditors, users, and academics interested in the decision-making processes underlying reported numbers as well as standard setters as they consider whether to provide additional guidance.

papers.title: Attraction and Departure of Early-Career Auditors: A Systematic Literature Review
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS This paper synthesizes research on the attraction and departure of early-career auditors (i.e., interns, staff, and senior associates). I develop a framework to organize the literature around determinants and consequences of attraction to and departure from the profession. Using this framework, I review evidence on the factors that shape entry into auditing, the characteristics of auditors and their work that influence turnover, and the outcomes of turnover for audits, the profession, firms, and individuals. I consider these findings against the backdrop of contemporary contextual factors, specifically regulatory pressures, evolving work arrangements, emerging technology, and gender. The literature shows that early-career experiences are central to the stability and sustainability of the audit pipeline and reveals how interconnected factors influence both attraction and departure. I conclude by identifying promising directions for future research that address gaps in understanding the determinants and consequences of early-career auditors’ experiences. JEL Classifications: M42.

papers.title: A Decade Later: The Changing Landscape of Non-GAAP Reporting
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS We provide evidence on recent trends in managers’ non-GAAP reporting. First, the rapid increase in non-GAAP earnings disclosures identified in prior research has leveled off in recent years. Moreover, managers are more likely to provide these non-GAAP metrics in concert with analysts, and instances in which only managers report non-GAAP metrics have declined. Managers exclude both nonrecurring and recurring items more frequently in the recent decade, and the magnitude of their recurring item exclusions has dramatically increased. Finally, we find that exclusion persistence has increased in the recent decade and is significant, regardless of whether or not analysts corroborate managers’ metrics. We also find that the lowest quality non-GAAP reporting still occurs when managers report non-GAAP earnings while analysts do not. It is important to recognize, however, that non-GAAP earnings remain considerably more persistent than non-GAAP exclusions, suggesting that non-GAAP earnings still provide meaningful information about core performance. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M40; M41; M48.

papers.title: Risk Governance: A Way to Promote Ethical Business in Organizations
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Regulators seek to make organizations more ethical by imposing requirements for risk governance. However, the academic and practitioner literature questions whether regulators’ objective has been met. In this paper, based on a field study in the financial services industry, we describe innovative practices in risk governance at three companies that seem to have succeeded in mitigating some of their ethical issues. We thereby contribute to the practice of risk governance and show that risk governance can indeed foster ethics. Data Availability: Data consists of our confidential notes from the field visits. JEL Classifications: M40; K20; G32.

papers.title: The Accounting Pipeline Challenge: Insights from Accounting Firm Leaders
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS We interview 14 accounting firm leaders to understand the accounting pipeline challenge from the profession’s perspective. The interviews confirm some prior findings about the pipeline and offer new insights in four areas. First, interviewees do not view the shortage uniformly, including mixed views on the quality of entrants and interviewees viewing the shortage as more severe for the profession than for their firm. Second, interviewees indicate that the shortage is associated with many consequences within firms (e.g., increased workload and stress). Third, interviewees suggest that traditional responses to the shortage, such as higher compensation and enhanced retention strategies, may be reaching their limit. Finally, interviewees suggest that the profession is seeking new solutions to the shortage, including managing artificial intelligence (AI) versus human factors. We also find notable differences between major market/Big 4 firms and other firms. We discuss implications and future research directions in this rapidly changing environment.

papers.title: ESG in Executive Pay: Prevalence, Design, Role Alignment, and Gaps
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Using named executive officer (NEO)-level data for Russell 3000 firms from 2021 to 2024, we describe how firms incorporate environmental, social, and governance (ESG) metrics into executive compensation. ESG pay design varies across industries and executive functions in ways broadly consistent with incentive compatibility. However, ESG metrics remain concentrated in short-term incentive plans and are rarely embedded in equity awards. Explicit weights are much more common than modifiers, limiting the extent to which ESG performance affects total pay. In emission-intensive industries, firms quantify goals more often than reported outcomes, creating asymmetry between ex ante expectation and ex post performance. Overall, ESG-linked pay exhibits substantial role alignment, but important design gaps remain. The evidence provides benchmarks for compensation committees designing ESG pay, investors, and stakeholders evaluating pay practices, regulators, and researchers evaluating ESG-linked compensation. Data Availability: Data are commercially available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M40; M41.

papers.title: Discretionary Impairments of Finite and Indefinite Intangible Assets
papers.abstract: SYNOPSIS Motivated by the debate on how post-acquisition accounting should treat different types of intangibles, particularly the choice between amortization and impairment versus impairment-only approaches, we use hand-collected data on acquired intangible assets and their impairments to examine the determinants of impairments of finite and indefinite intangible assets and goodwill. Impairments of indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill are more strongly associated with reporting-related conditions than are impairments of finite-lived intangibles, which also exhibit modest associations with economic impairment indicators. Moreover, internal governance mechanisms moderate the relation between impairment pressure and recognized impairments for indefinite-lived intangibles and goodwill, but much less so for finite-lived intangibles, consistent with greater scope for discretion under the impairment-only regime. Our results are relevant for policymakers considering proposals to subsume intangible assets into goodwill and modify impairment test procedures. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text.

papers.title: Critical accountants in the face of ecological crises: towards a more-than-human critical resilience
The critical foundations of truly sustainable environmental auditing
Recent Reforms of Intergovernmental Grants for Local Governments in Germany: Consequences for Accountability and Oversight
papers.abstract: Germany's intergovernmental grant system faces mounting complexity and administrative burden. Recent reforms seek to reduce bureaucracy through lump‐sum funding, decentralized audits, and outcome‐focused approaches. Drawing on Second Generation Fiscal Federalism Theory and program implementation research, this article analyzes three reform cases: climate protection grants, audit decentralization in North Rhine‐Westphalia, and social block grants in Saxony. We identify a critical trade‐off: Simplification efforts enhance procedural efficiency but may weaken oversight and accountability. The findings reveal that reform design determines whether accountability gaps emerge. We conclude that formular‐based allocation, indicator‐based evaluation, or decentralized audit capacity can balance flexibility with accountability in a less bureaucratic fiscal environment.

papers.title: Enabling “Programmatic Formalizations”: How Local Actors in the Public Sector Address Wicked Problems Through External Initiatives
papers.abstract: Society faces wicked problems, that is, complex challenges that require sustained, multi‐actor collaboration. Actors at international, national, and regional levels support local action on wicked problems through various initiatives, which often make available concrete formalized supports that local actors can draw upon in practice. We conceptualize such supports as programmatic formalizations. However, the literature lacks a systematic understanding of how these formalized supports become actionable in local efforts. To address this gap, we draw on enabling control theory as an analytical lens in a qualitative study of actors responsible for preventive work that supports children at risk of not having a safe childhood in municipalities within a Swedish region. We illustrate the challenges these actors encounter and whether, when and how programmatic formalizations help address these issues. We further show how local actors draw on multiple programmatic formalizations to establish an organizational space, adapt local work, and develop routines that support collaboration. These actors also express doubts about sustaining such organizational space over time, given challenges related to financing and political attention. Based on these findings, we reinterpret enabling control by extending its scope from a focus on internally embedded organizational formalizations to a field of multiple, externally developed and non‐mandatory formalizations.

papers.title: How Territorial Financial Governance Complicates Vertical Relationships in the Multi‐National United Kingdom
papers.abstract: The United Kingdom is an asymmetric polity, in part because it is a multi‐national state brought together by conquest and voluntary union. The 1998 devolution settlements for Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland were conceived and implemented in the context of UK membership of the European Union (EU). This constitutional context conditioned the implementation of vertical public service reforms, including the accounting components of New Public Management which are powerful vertical integrators. To analyse the tensions between vertical public service reforms desired by centres of government and political pressures for territorial differentiation, economization's four “roles” of accounting are interacted with the four “modes” of government accounting. Divergence and similarities between the United Kingdom, England, and the devolved nations in accounting are analysed: accrual accounting, funding model, spending control, ex‐ante scrutiny, and public audit. Accounting plays a central role in territorializing polities and in mediating relationships between tiers of government and political actors. Accounting adjudicates processes and results, relying on “independent” institutions now vulnerable to increasingly aggressive higher‐tier governments which claim superior democratic mandates as justification for subjectivizing lower‐tier governments.

papers.title: Organizational Innovativeness in Bureaucratic Settings: The Role of Culture, Leadership, and Political Climate
papers.abstract: Despite innovation being a key trait for addressing public sector challenges, research on public sector innovation is disparate and lacks theoretical grounding. Grounded in innovation and organizational development literature, this article tests a cultural‐leadership model of organizational innovativeness using panel data (2011, 2014, and 2017) from the Canadian Public Service Employee Survey, comprising 422,073 respondents. The results showcase that cultural values of stability and supportiveness are the strongest enablers of innovativeness, whereas performance‐oriented values have weaker effects. Transformational leadership significantly promotes innovativeness and mitigates the negative influence of organizational inertia. Political climate exerts only marginal effects, suggesting that internal organizational factors outweigh external political pressures. These findings advance theory supporting an instrumental perspective of public organizations and establishing the central role of leadership in fostering innovation‐conducive cultural traits. Policy implications include prioritizing supportive organizational climates, leadership development, and inclusive innovation strategies over reliance on political or market‐driven reforms.

papers.title: Learning While Working: How Do Early Litigation Experiences Affect Managers’ Disclosure?
papers.abstract: We track the employment histories of over 6,000 chief executive officers (CEOs) and study how their past litigation experiences affect voluntary disclosure of management forecasts. We define litigation experience to be any securities class action experienced during a CEO’s early career in non-CEO positions and in other firms. We find that CEOs with litigation experience (“litigation CEOs”) provide more management forecasts. The positive effects are further identified using a matched sample design. We also find that litigation CEOs provide more timely forecasts, are more likely to provide range forecasts, and market reactions to their forecasts are stronger. Collectively, the evidence indicates that early career litigation exposure leads CEOs to improve both the quantity and quality of their voluntary disclosures.

papers.title: From Friends to Filings? Social Connectedness and the Demand for Public Information
papers.abstract: Exploiting social network data from Facebook, we show that investors acquire more publicly disclosed information about firms located in counties that are more socially connected to their home counties. Using significant information events as shocks to private communication within social networks, we find that this relation is stronger in the weeks leading up to these events, consistent with private communication via social networks stimulating investors’ demand for public information. The relation is also stronger when there is greater scope for complementarity between private communication and public information. Furthermore, we provide evidence that stock prices respond to earnings announcements more rapidly for firms headquartered in more socially connected counties, suggesting social networks improve price discovery. Overall, our study provides new insights into how social communication shapes investors’ acquisition of public information.

papers.title: Bank Risk-Taking and Deposits Around Going Concern Opinions
papers.abstract: We investigate bank risk-taking and deposit flows around first-time going concern opinions (GCOs). Although GCOs may strengthen market monitoring, they are also often accused of destabilizing banks by triggering depositor runs. Our evidence is difficult to reconcile with that concern. Uninsured deposits begin to decrease several quarters before the GCO, but insured deposits increase over the same period, leaving total deposits broadly stable around the opinion. This pattern suggests that more sophisticated depositors respond to timelier information than the annual audit report and shift from uninsured to insured funding before the GCO becomes public, whereas insured retail depositors do not exhibit large-scale withdrawals around the GCO. We also document that bank risk measures increase in the quarters leading up to the GCO and then stabilize and subsequently decrease after the opinion. In addition, severe enforcement actions become more likely in the post-GCO period. Taken together, these patterns are consistent with an indirect supervisory channel that may help interpret the post-GCO change in bank risk-taking. Overall, our findings suggest that concerns about GCOs precipitating depositor runs may be overstated and that systematic auditor forbearance is not clearly justified on financial-stability grounds.

papers.title: Modern slavery governance, digital transformation and financial distress risk: evidence from legally grounded text-based accounting measures
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to develop and validate a legally grounded accounting measurement framework for modern-slavery governance and examines whether the resulting governance measures are associated with firms' financial distress risk. Existing research predominantly relies on ESG ratings, disclosure proxies, or qualitative assessments that do not clearly distinguish externally specified governance obligations from firms' disclosed governance architecture. We address this measurement gap by translating mandatory modern-slavery governance requirements into reproducible firm-level accounting measures and evaluating their informational relevance for accounting-based risk assessment. Design/methodology/approach This research adopts a two-corpus measurement framework. The first corpus comprises mandatory modern-slavery legislation and internationally recognised institutional frameworks issued between 1930 and 2024, including the Tariff Act (1930), California Transparency in Supply Chains Act, UK Modern Slavery Act, French Duty of Vigilance Law, Australian Modern Slavery Act, German Supply Chain Due Diligence Act, Norwegian Transparency Act, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD), and complementary institutional frameworks including the ILO, OECD, PRI, and the United Nations Guiding Principles. Rather than serving as institutional background, these sources are used to define the governance construct by identifying legally codified organisational obligations and harmonising them into a unified governance ontology representing implementation-oriented governance mechanisms.The second corpus comprises more than 5,000 annual reports of S&P 500 firms covering the period 2010–2022. Artificial intelligence (AI), natural language processing (NLP), and supervised machine-learning techniques operationalise the predefined governance ontology to identify disclosed evidence of implementation-oriented governance mechanisms within corporate reports, thereby generating firm-year Modern Slavery Index (MSI) measures. A complementary Digital Transformation Index (DTI) captures disclosed digital capability. The empirical design combines firm and year fixed-effects estimation with 2SLS endogeneity-sensitivity analysis and additional tests addressing disclosure intensity and boilerplate reporting, institutional validity, digital-capability interactions, competing explanations and potential mechanisms. Findings The findings show that firms disclosing stronger implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance mechanisms exhibit lower financial distress risk, although the strength of this association varies across the underlying institutional architectures. Among the four governance measures, the California-based MSI2 provides the strongest evidence, indicating that disclosed governance mechanisms centred on supplier verification, monitoring, accountability, and supply-chain oversight are associated with lower financial distress risk. Digital transformation, by contrast, does not independently reduce financial distress risk and is associated with lower Altman Z-scores in several specifications, a pattern consistent with – but not establishing – the organisational costs and implementation challenges that may accompany technological transformation. Importantly, digital capability also conditions the association between disclosed modern-slavery governance and financial distress risk, with the positive MSI4 × DTI interaction indicating that the financial relevance of governance disclosure varies with firms' digital capabilities under particular institutional arrangements. Overall, the findings indicate that legally grounded measures of disclosed modern-slavery governance contain economically relevant information for financial-distress assessment, while their associations vary across governance architectures and according to firms' digital capabilities. Originality/value This paper makes four contributions to the accounting literature. First, it develops four transparent, legally grounded, and fully reproducible Modern Slavery Indices (MSI1–MSI4), each derived from distinct regulatory and institutional governance frameworks, providing researchers, practitioners, managers, auditors, and policymakers with standardised accounting measures of implementation-oriented modern-slavery governance. Second, it introduces a novel two-corpus measurement framework that explicitly separates construct definition from empirical observation by deriving the governance construct from mandatory legislation and internationally recognised frameworks before operationalising it through AI-enabled textual analysis of corporate reports. Third, it demonstrates how artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and supervised machine-learning techniques can operationalise externally defined governance obligations into scalable firm-level accounting information while preserving construct validity. Finally, it provides evidence that these legally grounded accounting measures contain decision-useful information for accounting-based risk assessment, advancing research on non-financial accounting measurement, governance architecture, disclosure credibility, internal control systems, and corporate resilience under emerging mandatory reporting regimes.

papers.title: Ethics and climate litigation: from case law to knowledge networks
papers.abstract: Purpose This article examines how climate litigation has evolved from a policy instrument into a legal mechanism for enforcing ethical obligations, positioning climate change as an ethical issue and identifying human rights as a litigation outcome. Design/methodology/approach Adopting the design of an integrative literature review, the study combines bibliometric mapping of Web of Science citation data, processed using Bibliometrix and Biblioshiny, with conceptual and doctrinal analysis of key climate litigation case law. Findings Climate change litigation is maturing not only in scope but in ethical grounding, with human rights emerging as a strategic outcome courts increasingly pursue. Using bibliometric analysis, this article maps the intersection of climate litigation and ethics, identifying five research areas: greenhouse gases as pollutants, duty of care, climate science, global climate policy and intercountry equity. Cross-jurisdictional themes show that judicial decisions do more than resolve individual disputes – they shape, legitimize and accelerate transnational governance responses to climate change, positioning courts as meaningful actors in addressing climate change as an ethical imperative. Social implications This study maps the acceptance of ethics within legal spheres as part of the climate debate. Originality/value The article is among the first to integrate bibliometric mapping with doctrinal and ethical analysis of climate litigation, and proposes a tiered research agenda that addresses the interplay between government objectives and the interests of litigants.

papers.title: Adapting to extreme heat: how corporate responses enhance customer stability
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper examines the impact of extreme heat risk on corporate customer stability in the Chinese market. Design/methodology/approach Using a comprehensive dataset from 2012 to 2023, we find that greater exposure to city-level extreme heat risk incentive firms to adopt adaptive adjustments, thereby enhancing customer stability. Findings This effect is mainly achieved through three channels, including optimizing human capital, advancing digital transformation and strengthening supply chain finance. Cross-sectional heterogeneity test reveals that the impact is more pronounced in firms with lower labor intensity, fewer high-skilled employees and limited trade credit access. These findings provide novel evidence on how firms transform climate-related risks into opportunities to strengthen resilience, and offer important implications for corporate adaptation strategies and policy support in the context of global climate change. Originality/value Our research makes several contributions in three major aspects. First and foremost, our findings extend the literature on the economic consequences of extreme heat; furthermore, our research enriches the literature on the determinants of customer stability; last but not least, by examining the mechanism linking extreme heat risks at firm locations to customer stability, our study extends organizational adaptation theory to the context of climate risk and supply chains, enriching the theoretical framework on how climate factors influence corporate supply chain networks.

papers.title: Covered interest rate parity in the presence of time-varying transaction costs: an application of the fractional integration approach
papers.abstract: Purpose We demonstrate that fractional integration offers an improved framework for assessing the reliability of the covered interest rate parity condition compared with traditional unit root tests. Specifically, in the presence of transaction costs, the parity condition will tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds, making the process fractionally integrated at that bound which renders traditional unit root tests unsuitable. Given the widespread adoption of parity conditions in practice, in areas such as risk management and foreign exchange rate forecasting, an approach which permits an assessment of the reliability of these models, particularly for volatile markets such as emerging markets, is crucial. Design/methodology/approach We propose a threshold autoregression framework that more effectively identifies near-unit-root behaviour and improves market classification relative to conventional approaches. The analysis uses data from the industrialized markets of Australia, Hong Kong, Japan, New Zealand and Singapore, as well as the emerging markets of India, Indonesia, Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines and Thailand, with the USA serving as the reference market. Findings Our results show that shocks to covered interest rate parity are asymmetric and that the parity conditions tend towards one of the arbitrage bounds. Originality/value The fractional integration approach is well established in the econometric literature, though we are the first to apply this in this context. In relation to the international finance literature on tests of parity, recent attention has been almost exclusively on the causes of parity deviations than on assessing the reliability of the condition as an exchange rate forecasting instrument.

papers.title: Do textual attributes of management commentary matter for analyst coverage and information quality: evidence from the United Kingdom
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether the readability of management commentary is associated with analysts' coverage and the precision of analysts' information sets. It further investigates whether analysts' experience, access to resources and forecast boldness moderate these relationships. Design/methodology/approach Using 5,117 firm-year observations from 974 UK-listed firms, we employ ordinary least squares (OLS) regression models to examine the association between management commentary readability and analyst outcomes. To address potential endogeneity concerns and assess the robustness of our findings, we conduct additional analyses using entropy balancing, the Heckman (1979) two-stage procedure, omitted variable bias analysis, instrumental variable estimation and alternative measures of readability. Findings We find that firms with less readable management commentary have greater analyst coverage and higher precision of analysts' information sets. Decomposing total information precision into public and private components, we find that lower readability is positively associated with both public and private information precision. These findings are consistent with lower readability increasing the value of analysts' information-processing and information-production activities and suggest that analysts respond to less readable commentary by both processing publicly available information and acquiring additional private information. We further show that analyst experience and forecast boldness strengthen the positive association between lower readability and both analyst coverage and information precision. In contrast, analysts' access to resources strengthens the association between lower readability and analyst coverage but does not significantly moderate the association with information precision. Additional analysis indicates that the component of textual complexity attributable to observable business complexity is positively associated with analyst coverage and with total and public information precision, but not with private information precision. Research limitations/implications The findings have implications for regulators, standard setters, firms and investors by highlighting the need to distinguish unnecessary complexity from textual complexity arising from economically relevant information. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on narrative disclosures readability and analyst behaviour by highlighting analysts' information-provider role and demonstrating that the association between management commentary readability and analyst outcomes varies with analysts' attributes, particularly their experience and forecast boldness.

papers.title: Do Modified Retrospective Transitions Facilitate Earnings Management? Evidence from ASU 2016-13
papers.abstract: This paper considers two related earnings/capital management opportunities available to banks as they transitioned to ASU 2016-13. Under the FASB’s transition guidance, banks estimate credit losses under the new standard and take the initial adoption adjustment (IAA) directly into retained earnings. Shifting pre-adoption provision accruals to their IAA buckets enables banks to increase their reported income in the period before adoption while avoiding regulatory scrutiny, since their allowances are increased promptly. Consistent with this hypothesized behavior, we find that banks making timely adoptions of ASU 2016-13 on 1/1/2020 reported more negative abnormal provision accruals in 2019 than nonadopting banks. Negative abnormal provision accruals in 2019 were associated with larger IAAs in Q1 of 2020. We also formulate and test competing hypotheses about banks’ decisions to delay adoption under the CARES Act (U.S. Congress 2020). We find that adoption delays are associated with size-related adoption challenges rather than earnings management. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; G21.

papers.title: A Framework for Mitigating the Effects of Large Number Innumeracy in Corporate Disclosures
papers.abstract: As corporate disclosures increasingly report figures in the millions, billions, and trillions, large number innumeracy may systematically distort how investors interpret firm performance. This cognitive limitation arises when individuals compress large magnitudes on the mental number line, overestimating absolute values while underestimating differences between them. We introduce large number innumeracy as a distinct perceptual construct in the accounting literature and synthesize cognitive science and accounting research to explain how it may affect investor interpretation of corporate disclosures and why susceptibility likely varies across investor types. We develop a mitigation framework organized by how directly each mechanism addresses the problem: direct approaches alter how values are represented, contextual supports aid interpretation without changing magnitude representation, and interpretive intermediaries shift processing to outside actors or automated tools. We conclude with a research agenda on prevalence, capital market consequences, and mitigation, with implications for disclosure design, investor protection, and market efficiency. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; G41; D91; D83.

Do investors equally value women directors? Evidence from financial expertise
AI Disclosure, Signal Quality and Washing: Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
papers.abstract: Using Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2016 to 2024, we examine whether Firm‐Specific AI Disclosure predicts subsequent observable AI activity and when disclosure becomes disconnected from action. AI disclosure is most consistently associated with future patenting, while evidence for hiring and broader capital investment is shorter‐lived, supporting an informative‐but‐imperfect signal interpretation. We define AI washing as multidimensional disclosure–action mismatch and find that greater mismatch is associated with AI‐specific stock‐exchange scrutiny. However, inquiry is not followed by broad and persistent realignment: fewer than half of classifiable responses meet our Substantive‐Evidence threshold, consistent with a Detection–Correction Gap.

papers.title: Supply Chain Digital Transformation Misalignment and Supplier Greenwashing: A Dual‐Path Perspective
papers.abstract: Supply chain digital transformation often progresses unevenly across upstream and downstream partners, creating digital transformation misalignment. Drawing on the ability‐motivation‐opportunity (AMO) framework, this study examines how such misalignment affects supplier greenwashing and develops a dual‐path perspective to explain how different directions of digital asymmetry shape supplier responses. Using data on Chinese supply‐chain relationships, we find that supply chain digital transformation misalignment significantly increases supplier greenwashing. Further analyses reveal two distinct behavioural pathways. When suppliers lag behind customers in digital maturity, digital capability constraints limit their ability to undertake and substantiate substantive environmental actions, while relational and transactional pressures increase the incentives to demonstrate environmental responsibility, giving rise to a capability‐constrained symbolic response. In contrast, when suppliers outperform customers in digital maturity, superior information‐processing and information‐control capabilities can weaken customer monitoring and verification, creating opportunities for information‐enabled strategic decoupling. We further identify three mechanisms through which digital transformation misalignment facilitates supplier greenwashing: supply chain information asymmetry, transactional pressure and supervision gaps. In addition, buyer dependency and industry environmental sensitivity amplify the effect of digital transformation misalignment, whereas environmental regulation mitigates it. This study contributes to the supply chain sustainability literature by conceptualizing digital transformation misalignment as a form of sustainability governance imbalance and by demonstrating how different configurations of ability, motivation, and opportunity can generate supplier greenwashing through distinct behavioural pathways. The findings also provide implications for strengthening environmental information governance and monitoring in digitally fragmented supply networks.

papers.title: False Green, True Damage: The Erosion of Supplier Sustainability Through Greenwashing Spillovers in Supply Chains
papers.abstract: Using matched supplier–client data of Chinese A‐share listed companies (2009–2024), we examine how client greenwashing affects suppliers' green total factor productivity (GTFP). We find that client greenwashing significantly suppresses suppliers' GTFP, indicating that downstream firms' selective environmental communication can translate into real efficiency losses in upstream green production. This effect mainly operates through a weakened information environment and reduced supplier green efforts. Further analyses show that the effect is stronger when dependence asymmetry is more pronounced or more difficult to mitigate, namely when clients have greater market influence, when client information transparency is lower, or when suppliers have a lower degree of digital transformation. Our findings reveal that selective environmental communication generates spillover effects beyond disclosing firms, adversely impacting suppliers' green development.

papers.title: Investor Perspectives on Human Capital Disclosures: Australian Evidence
papers.abstract: This study investigates how Australian institutional and retail investors perceive, assess and utilise human capital information. Surveys of 100 and interviews with 11 investors indicate high perceived relevance but limited reported integration of human capital information in decision‐making. Institutional investors emphasised qualitative assessment and engagement, while retail investors relied on reputational cues. Participants expressed dissatisfaction with current disclosures and sought standardised, detailed and comparable metrics. The study extends sustainability disclosure research by highlighting investor‐related barriers and the specific disclosure improvements they seek, with implications for standard setters, regulators and preparers aiming to improve the decision‐usefulness of human capital reporting.

papers.title: Correction to ‘ CEO Organizational Identification and Corporate Innovation Investment’
Information Disclosure Transformation in the Digital Economy: The Role of Digital Infrastructure in Visual Disclosure
papers.abstract: We investigate how digital infrastructure development affects corporate visual disclosure, distinguishing between discretionary image‐based formats and structured table‐based formats. Using data on Chinese A‐share‐listed firms from 2009 to 2022, we find that improvements in digital infrastructure are associated with greater use of image‐based visual disclosure in annual reports, whereas we detect no statistically significant association with table‐based visual disclosure. Mechanism analyses show that this relationship is driven by both supply‐side enhancements in firms' organizational capabilities and demand‐side incentives to cater to external users' information‐processing demands, as evidenced by stronger effects among firms with more extensive explicit discussions of digital transformation in their MD&A and higher institutional ownership. We also find that this effect is more pronounced in regions with higher levels of AI computing power development, as well as among firms with a lower propensity for earnings manipulation and fewer financing constraints. This paper expands the theoretical framework for understanding changes in corporate disclosure formats in the digital economy and offers implications for policymakers, investors and firms.

papers.title: Central State‐Owned Enterprise Ownership and Local State‐Owned Enterprise Innovation: Evidence From China
papers.abstract: This study examines a previously unexplored corporate governance mechanism, that is, the presence of central state‐owned enterprises (SOEs) as non‐controlling shareholders in local SOEs in China, and investigates its impact on corporate innovation. Our research reveals that central SOE ownership enhances local SOE innovation. Further analyses based on the 2016 top‐down innovation‐related policy and policy uncertainty provide additional evidence that central SOE ownership serves as a channel for transmitting policy information to local SOEs and improves their innovation. Moreover, we show that central SOE ownership and private ownership function as complements in fostering innovation of local SOEs. The positive effect of central SOE ownership, however, is attenuated by stronger local government intervention and greater geographic distance between local and central SOEs. Overall, our findings highlight the governance role of central SOE ownership, attributable to its higher hierarchical position within the political system. By illuminating the role of shareholder identity and political hierarchy, this study contributes to the literature on non‐controlling shareholders and extends research on the heterogeneity of state ownership, thereby offering important implications for SOE governance.

papers.title: Unpacking Modern Slavery in Business Research: Conceptualization and Operationalization
papers.abstract: Despite the tragic humanitarian impact of modern slavery, modern slavery research is underdeveloped and advancing slowly. Theoretical studies abound, while there are few quantitative studies with large‐scale empirical evidence to test theory. We review the literature to better understand how modern slavery has been defined and measured. We find a wide discrepancy among conceptual definitions of modern slavery. Only a few studies operationalize (measure) modern slavery. To aid conceptual clarity, we develop a tentative business‐related definition of modern slavery based on our review. We also identify six data sources and several opportunities for quantitative research to benefit researchers and practitioners. JEL Classification: M14, M49

papers.title: Customer Concentration and Abnormal Management Tone: Perspectives From Private Information Transmission
papers.abstract: This study examines the relation between customer concentration and abnormal management tone using a sample of Chinese A‐share listed firms from 2007 to 2021. We find that customer concentration is negatively associated with abnormal management tone. Mechanism analyses suggest that firms with higher customer concentration rely more on private information channels to communicate with their major customers. Cross‐sectional analyses show that this negative association is stronger when firms provide more trade credit or have higher inventory management efficiency, but does not vary significantly with internal or external monitoring. Overall, this study contributes to a better understanding of the role of customer relationships in firms' qualitative disclosure strategies.

papers.title: The Effects of Accounting Enforcement on the Informativeness of Capitalised R&D Across IFRS Countries
papers.abstract: We examine the effect of country‐level accounting enforcement on the informativeness of capitalised R&D across 19 countries that adopted IFRS by 2005. We find that capitalised R&D has a marginally stronger positive association with future earnings in strong‐enforcement countries compared to weak‐enforcement countries, consistent with higher financial reporting quality for R&D in more rigorous enforcement environments. We also find that the association between capitalised R&D and market value is weaker in countries with stronger enforcement. This finding is consistent with stronger enforcement environments providing enhanced narrative disclosures that may convey some of the R&D‐related information directly to investors, thereby reducing the incremental valuation role of the capitalised R&D.

papers.title: A Journey From the GFC to the COVID ‐19 Pandemic: Does Corporate Leaders' Learning in One Crisis Matter in Another?
papers.abstract: We examine whether executives' and directors' collective learning from the Global Financial Crisis (GFC) enhanced firm resilience during the COVID‐19 crisis. Drawing on learning transfer theory, we argue that knowledge acquired during one crisis influences subsequent corporate policies and outcomes. Using a sample of U.S. firms, we find that greater GFC experience among leadership teams is associated with superior firm performance in 2020. Additional analyses indicate that lessons learned during the GFC shaped post‐crisis corporate decisions, which contributed to stronger performance during the pandemic. Overall, our findings highlight the value of collective learning and knowledge transfer in strengthening organizational resilience.

Audit Team Paradox‐in‐Virtuality and Audit Quality Threatening Behaviour
papers.abstract: This study investigates the association between audit team virtuality and audit quality‐threatening behaviour (AQTB). Although virtuality theory suggests that high virtuality can hinder team interactions, virtuality‐in‐paradox theory shows such tools can simultaneously create isolation and efficiency, reduce interpersonal bias and empower timely task completion. This suggests that structural and perceived aspects of virtuality have a more complex influence on team behaviour. Paradox‐in‐virtuality theory is applied to explain how virtuality affects audit team behaviour. Data were collected from 335 auditors across 185 audit team engagements at a Big 4 audit firm using a questionnaire survey. Ordered logistic regression analysis and robustness tests are applied. Results show that audit team virtuality is associated with AQTB. Teams that rely more heavily on communication technologies report higher levels of AQTB, whereas teams experiencing greater synchronicity and higher information quality report lower levels of AQTB. However, the interaction analyses reveal important nuances: When synchronicity occurs together with high technology use, AQTB increases, but when information quality is high, whether combined with technology use or with synchronicity, AQTB becomes less frequent. The consequences are analysed, and future research prospects are discussed. This research contributes to audit quality and audit team literature by identifying determinants of AQTB at the team level. Insights into audit team behaviour are valuable for practitioners adapting to new communication technologies. Contributions are made to team virtuality research and behavioural outcomes by testing its three dimensions in professional audit practice.

papers.title: Are Unaudited Firms More Likely to Disregard Tax Payments Prior to Bankruptcy? Small‐Firm Evidence From Sweden
papers.abstract: Proponents of mandatory auditing claim that auditing reduces the risk of tax evasion and that firms disregarding tax payments distort competition because they operate with lower costs than firms that meet their tax obligations. To investigate this, we analyse data from a credit reference agency to examine whether unaudited firms are more likely than audited firms to fail to pay income taxes and value‐added taxes up to 4 years prior to bankruptcy. We also examine the association between auditing and tax avoidance prior to bankruptcy and find mixed results, with some evidence suggesting that audited firms engage in greater tax avoidance than unaudited firms. In conclusion, our results indicate that auditing is associated with a higher likelihood of tax‐payment compliance among failing firms. At the same time, we find only limited evidence that auditing systematically affects tax avoidance behaviour or increases tax revenues through higher tax payments.

Eponymous Family Firms’ Reputation Concerns and Auditor Choice: Evidence from the FTSE Italia All-Share
papers.abstract: Considering family firm heterogeneity and drawing on signaling theory, we examine how family firms’ reputation concerns impact their auditor choices. The sample comprises 891 family firm year observations, for 96 family firms, extracted from 132 Italian nonfinancial listed firms, and for the period 2010 to 2020. Using eponymy as our proxy for family firms with stronger reputation concerns, as expected, we find that compared to noneponymous family firms, eponymous family firms are associated with higher quality auditors (Big 4 auditors and audit industry specialists). This association is robust to a battery of sensitivity and robustness tests, including alternative definitions of family firms and alternative measures of audit industry specialization. Cross-sectional tests further show that the association persists across both stronger and weaker internal corporate governance environments, suggesting that the reputational signaling role of eponymy is not dependent on specific internal governance configurations. Data Availability: Data used in this study were collected from publicly available sources. JEL Classifications: G34; M42.

papers.title: The integration between Sustainability Management Systems (SMS) and Sustainability Management Accounting Controls (SMCS): a review of contemporary literature and implications for future research
papers.abstract: This paper aims to synthesise insights into the relationship between Sustainability Management Systems (SMS) and Sustainability Management Control Systems (SMCS). Specifically, it presents a framework that illustrates the dynamic interplay between sustainability systems and control mechanisms. This study employs a systematic literature review approach to explore key themes and significant findings in this rapidly evolving field. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines for selecting journal articles, this paper presents a comprehensive analysis of 92 published studies on sustainability management systems and sustainability management controls. Based on an in-depth qualitative analysis, this paper proposes a conceptual framework to synthesise the integration of the Management Control Package Framework and the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle. This study also identifies mechanisms suggested by previous literature on SMS and SMCS integration under technical, organisational, and cognitive dimensions. Overall, this study represents one of the earliest attempts to highlight the crossovers between two related concepts within a single framework for analysis. This paper presents relevant sources of knowledge, literature on the topic, relevant authors, and other valuable information to assist interested researchers in better understanding the field. This systematic literature review can support researchers and practitioners in the field of sustainability management by setting out avenues for future research. This study highlights the potential of integrating SMS and SMCS to strengthen sustainability governance in business organisations.

papers.title: Guardians of governance: the role of auditor industry specialization in mitigating corporate misconduct through internal controls
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the impact of statutory auditor industry specialization on corporate misconduct in China’s A-share market, with a specific focus on the mediating role of internal control quality in mitigating corporate misconduct. Design/methodology/approach Using a sample of 3,794 firms (2010-2022), we apply fixed-effects regression models and a two-stage least squares (2SLS) approach to address potential endogeneity. We quantify auditor industry specialization using market share, while the occurrence and frequency of regulatory violations are used to measure corporate misconduct. Findings The results show that auditors with industry specialization significantly reduce both the likelihood and frequency of corporate misconduct. Furthermore, internal control quality serves as a significant mediating mechanism in the relationship between auditor industry specialization and corporate misconduct. These findings highlight the role of industry specialized auditors as vital external governance agents, particularly in firms with concentrated ownership or those operating in highly competitive industries. Practical implications This study highlights policy implications for regulators and policymakers, recommending the development of auditor industry specialization through certification programs and stricter industry-specific auditing standards. Firms should engage industry-specialized auditors and invest in resources and training to improve the quality of internal controls. Originality/value This research significantly contributes to the corporate governance and auditing literature by highlighting that auditor industry specialization serves as a key external disciplinary mechanism that enhances the effectiveness of internal control. It also contributes to agency and resource-based theories by highlighting the critical role of auditor industry specialization and internal control in detecting and preventing corporate misconduct.

papers.title: Audit committees and climate risk disclosure: a transformer-based textual analysis approach
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether audit committee (AC) attributes are associated with the extent of climate risk disclosure in mandated US annual reports, distinguishing between physical- and transition-risk discussion in 10-K Item 1A (Risk Factors). Design/methodology/approach Using S&P 500 firms, the study extracts Item 1A from 10-K filings and applies a transformer-based NLP classifier (ClimateBERT) to score firm-year physical- and transition-risk disclosure. Multiple regression models and alternative proxies are used to test the robustness of results. Findings The results show that AC independence, gender diversity and expertise are associated with higher physical- and transition-risk disclosure, consistent with stronger monitoring and closer review of climate-related narratives in 10-K filings. Longer committee tenure is linked to lower disclosure, suggesting that familiarity with management may soften scrutiny over time. The presence of an AC is also associated with higher disclosure. These results are stronger in carbon-intensive sectors and remain stable across multiple robustness tests. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to large US non-financial firms (S&P 500), which may restrict generalizability. The dependent variables are disclosure-based measures derived from textual classification of Item 1A and reflect how risks are communicated rather than underlying exposure. Practical implications Boards, AC chairs and investors can expect AC composition to shape the depth and clarity of climate-risk discussion in 10-K risk factors. Independence, gender mix and expertise are linked to fuller narratives that help users assess physical hazards and transition pressures. Regulators may also view AC features as part of the reporting system that helps explain cross-firm differences in climate-risk communication under a common US regime. Originality/value The study connects AC design to climate-risk disclosure in Form 10-K filings by using transformer-based text analytics that separate physical from transition risk within Item 1A. This provides fresh evidence on how reporting oversight relates to emerging-risk narratives and offers a scalable method for governance–disclosure research.

papers.title: Negative press coverage, litigation risk, and audit opinions in China
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether and why auditors are more likely to issue modified audit opinions (MAOs) to clients receiving negative news reports. Design/methodology/approach Exploiting a legal regime change in China in 2005 that significantly increased auditor litigation risk, the authors divide the sample period into two subperiods: the low litigation risk period (2001–2004) and the high litigation risk period (2006–2009). The authors manually read and code all newspapers to identify firm-years in which clients received negative press coverage. To address endogeneity and self-selection concerns, the authors use propensity score matching, instrumental variable estimation and Heckman’s two-stage model. Findings This study finds that auditors are more likely to issue MAOs to clients receiving negative news reports in the high litigation risk period. In particular, auditors’ MAOs are positively related to the first negative news reports, accounting-related negative press coverage and negative news reports from state-owned media in the high litigation risk period. Further analysis shows that negative news reports increase the probability of covered firms receiving regulatory sanctions or getting sued. As a strategic defense, auditors can reduce the probability of being sued and making litigation payments by issuing MAOs in the high litigation risk period. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is the first to provide comprehensive evidence in support of the strategic view and its implications (negative news reports increase the probability of covered firms getting sued and auditors can mitigate litigation risk by issuing MAOs).

papers.title: Bullwhip ripples in external assurance: supply chain risks and auditor responses
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how amplified fluctuations in supply and demand (the bullwhip effect) influence auditors’ risk assessments and pricing decisions. By examining whether operational instabilities spill over into external audit fees and disclosures, it aims to clarify the role of supply chain volatility as a key determinant in the audit environment. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a large sample of Chinese listed firms, the authors construct firm-specific measures of the bullwhip effect by calculating the ratio of the volatility of production to the volatility of demand. These measures are then merged with annual audit-fee data and textual analyses of key audit matters (KAM) in audit reports. A quasi-natural experiment exploiting China’s intelligent supply chain policy is used to address potential endogeneity. Findings The results show that heightened supply–demand imbalances are significantly associated with higher audit fees, indicating that auditors perceive and price in this operational volatility as engagement risk. The findings also reveal that, under more pronounced bullwhip distortions, auditors devote greater attention to supply chain–related disclosures in the KAM section, suggesting that operational risks now occupy a central place in external assurance considerations. Originality/value By integrating a critical operational factor into traditional audit fee models, this study broadens the understanding of how real-side inefficiencies shape external assurance costs and disclosures. The evidence underscores the importance of supply chain dynamics in auditors’ risk evaluations and highlights how policy interventions aimed at stabilizing supply chain operations can mitigate upstream auditing expenses and informational frictions.

papers.title: Quarterly reporting timeliness as an early signal of reporting and internal control risk
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the significance of quarterly report lag as a potential indicator of firms’ annual reporting timeliness and internal control issues, informing policymakers about the incremental value of quarterly reports beyond other well-documented attributes. Design/methodology/approach Following Blankley et al. (2014), the authors use a two-stage approach to estimate a quarterly lag model and then examine the incremental information embedded in the unexplained (abnormal) component of quarterly report lag (AQRL). Findings Based on a sample of the US firms from 2007 to 2023, the authors find that AQRL predicts annual report lag and positively relates to the likelihood of internal control weaknesses. Additional analysis shows that the informational value of AQRL is mainly concentrated among the firms with Big 4 auditors, suggesting that quarterly reporting delays are more informative when audit processes are more standardized and stringent. Originality/value This study responds to the call by Kajüter et al. (2022) that researchers should investigate the impact of quarterly reports on “the time needed to perform the annual audit,” contributing to both interim financial reporting and reporting timeliness literature streams. While prior research mainly focuses on the frequency, content and assurance of quarterly financial reporting, the authors concentrate on the timeliness aspect that conveys useful information about the auditor, the client and the reporting process.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence and corporate green transformation: evidence from China’s A-share listed firms
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how artificial intelligence (AI) adoption contributes to corporate green transformation. It analyses the mediating roles of green technological innovation and human capital upgrading, the moderating roles of organisational resilience and environmental regulation and the heterogeneous effects across industrial and regional contexts. Design/methodology/approach This study uses panel data on Chinese A-share listed non-financial firms from 2008 to 2023. Fixed-effects regressions, instrumental-variable estimation, propensity score matching, mediation analysis, interaction models and subgroup analyses are used to examine the relationship between AI adoption and corporate green transformation, its transmission mechanisms, boundary conditions and contextual heterogeneity. Findings AI adoption is positively associated with corporate green transformation, and the result remains robust to alternative measures and endogeneity tests. Green technological innovation and human capital upgrading partially mediate this relationship, while organisational resilience and environmental regulation strengthen it. The positive relationship is statistically significant among firms in non-heavily polluting industries, firms in eastern and western China and firms in non-resource-based cities, but not in the corresponding comparison groups. Originality/value This study extends recent evidence on the environmental effects of AI by explaining how AI adoption is converted into firm-level green transformation and why this process varies across firms and locations. It provides an integrated account of the technological, workforce, organisational, institutional and structural conditions that shape the environmental value of AI adoption.

papers.title: The relationships between geopolitical risk, the value relevance of accounting information and auditor opinion: evidence from a developing market
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the relationship between geopolitical risk (GPR) and the value relevance (VR) of accounting information (AI) under different types of auditor opinion (AO). Design/methodology/approach This study uses a sample of nonfinancial firms listed on EGX100 during the period 2014–2023. Whereas GPR and AO data have been collected manually from annual reports and governance reports, stock prices are collected from EGX Archives available at the Egyptian Company for Information Dissemination. The study depends on the t-test, Pearson correlation, and OLS, 2SLS and GMM regressions to examine the authors’ hypotheses. Findings The results revealed a negative effect of GPR on the VR of AI. However, this negative effect may vary across accounting measures, depending on the auditor’s opinion. The VR of book value (BVS) declined during higher GPR periods, which was clearly visible with qualified auditor opinion. However, GPR increased the value relevance of EPS, which was clearly visible with unqualified auditor opinion, indicating that EPS might be perceived as a more reliable measure in uncertain environments, especially with the existence of a supportive auditor opinion. Originality/value This study contributes to literature by examining relationships between geopolitical risk, the VR of AI and auditor opinion, especially in developing markets, such as the Egyptian stock market. This study has practical implications, which can guide emerging market firms facing challenges during GPR periods to improve market perceptions about the firm.

papers.title: Caught in the crossfire: Geopolitical risk and firm performance, and the lifeline of risk management and sustainability strategies
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to test the adverse impact of geopolitical risk (GP_RISK) on firm performance and to examine whether risk management and sustainability strategies mitigate this relationship in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. Design/methodology/approach The study sample comprises 6140 firm-year observations from non-financial listed firms from 2013 to 2024. Consistent with prior studies, the study uses a system GMM estimator to address endogeneity and heterogeneity issues in panel data, ensuring consistent and efficient estimates. Findings The study shows that heightened GP_RISK significantly reduces firm performance in the GCC, negatively affecting both return on assets (ROA) and Tobin’s Q. The adverse effect is stronger for ROA, indicating that geopolitical shocks transmit more immediately through operational channels, including higher adjustment costs, supply-chain disruptions and operational inefficiencies. The negative impact on Tobin’s Q reflects investors’ concerns regarding future performance and risk exposure. The findings further show that geographical diversification (GEO_DIV) intensifies the adverse effect of GP_RISK, while hedging does not significantly mitigate it. In contrast, environmental, social and governance performance reduces the negative impact of GP_RISK, driven primarily by the governance dimension. Originality/value This study contributes to research on GP_RISK and firm-level dynamics in the emerging GCC context. It integrates political risk, risk management and stakeholder theories to explore the relationship between GP_RISK and firm performance and to evaluate the shielding effect of risk management and sustainability strategies. The research offers several important theoretical and practical implications for emerging economies.

papers.title: Financial support or innovation hindrance? Impact of venture capital’s discounted subscription in private placements on corporate innovation
papers.abstract: Purpose Venture capital (VC) participation in private placements may support innovation, but high subscription discounts can distort investor incentives and discourage long-term innovation. This study aims to examine how subscription discounts shape the innovation effects of VC participation. Design/methodology/approach Using China A-share listed firms from 2006 to 2023, this study examines the mechanisms and economic consequences of VC participation and subscription discounts in private placements. Findings VC participation in discounted private placements significantly weakens firms’ innovation capabilities. This effect operates through reduced R&D investment and increased inefficient investment and is more pronounced under greater information asymmetry. It is also stronger for mature and industry-focused VC investors, firms located in regions with greater capital concentration, growth-stage firms and financially constrained firms. Further analyses indicate that VC investors subscribing at higher discounts exhibit a stronger financial orientation. Under low-discount conditions, better innovation performance is associated with a lower likelihood of subsequent VC divestment, whereas this relationship disappears under high-discount conditions. Discounted subscriptions by VC investors also impair firms’ long-term stock market performance. Originality/value This study extends the VC short-termism literature by identifying entry-stage pricing as a determinant of VC incentives and corporate innovation.

papers.title: Can ChatGPT be skeptical? A case-based evaluation of generative AI in financial statement auditing
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how effectively GenAI (ChatGPT) displays professional skepticism characteristics in external audit tasks, as insufficient skepticism may impair audit quality and heighten the risk of audit failure. Design/methodology/approach ChatGPT is evaluated using four audit tasks representing common judgment-oriented audit procedures. Three experienced external auditors independently assessed ChatGPT’s responses using a structured professional skepticism assessment. Findings ChatGPT appears to display varying levels of skepticism characteristics across audit tasks, with relatively higher levels in preliminary risk assessments and substantive analytical procedures and lower levels in going-concern evaluations. This suggests that it may be more effective in analytical tasks than in those requiring deeper professional judgment. Originality/value This study appears to be among the first to systematically assess whether a general-purpose reasoning GenAI tool can display characteristics associated with professional skepticism across different audit tasks. By applying an established skepticism framework, it provides a structured baseline for understanding where GenAI may support or fall short in audit judgment contexts.

papers.title: Cryptocurrencies and the Future of Money as a Public Good
papers.abstract: This article engages with Digital Assets and the Law to examine the implications of digital monetary innovations, including cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and CBDCs, for the institutional foundations of contemporary monetary systems. It argues that these innovations bring into sharper focus fundamental questions about the purposes of money and whether existing public-private institutional arrangements remain adequate to fulfil them. Rather than viewing crypto-assets as exogenous developments, the article situates them within a broader historical and political context, tracing their emergence to longstanding tensions in monetary governance. Focusing primarily on policy responses in Western economies, it argues that many have been predominantly conservative, seeking to preserve and adapt the existing monetary order rather than addressing the underlying tensions from which these innovations emerged. Instead, the article proposes assessing alternative monetary arrangements according to their capacity to strengthen money’s character as a public good. It concludes by outlining five possible future scenarios, evaluating each in terms of their implications for monetary governance and the broader public interest.
