NRBV's strategic capabilities and SDG disclosure: Does this disclosure enhance financial performance?
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to extend the sustainable development goals (SDG) disclosure literature by examining the influence of natural resource-based view (NRBV) strategic capabilities, namely pollution prevention, green product innovation and environmental certification, on SDG disclosure practices among Indonesian companies. It also investigates the association between this disclosure and financial performance. Design/methodology/approach This study uses Indonesian companies listed in Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) for the period 2021 to 2024, comprising 1,256 company-year observations from 314 companies. All data for the variables are collected from annual and sustainability reports and analyzed using panel regression. Findings This study demonstrates that NRBV-based strategic capabilities, such as pollution prevention, green product innovation and environmental certification, significantly enhance companies' SDG disclosure. However, such disclosure is associated with lower financial performance due to the substantial costs required to support SDG-related activities. Practical implications The findings of this study provide practical implications for regulators as the commitment for achieving the SDG can be actualized through stricter sustainability regulations. It can be used to encourage companies to integrate strategic capabilities provided by NRBV into business operations. Originality/value This study extends the existing literature on SDG disclosure by shifting the focus from commonly examined governance and ownership determinants to the role of NRBV's strategic capabilities. It further contributes by examining the implications of SDG disclosure for companies' financial performance within an emerging market country context like Indonesia. This study also provides complementary evidence to prior studies predominantly conducted in developed countries.

papers.title: Bankruptcy system reform and shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises: evidence from China
papers.abstract: Purpose Bankruptcy system reform is an effective measure to improve judicial efficiency in bankruptcy proceedings and protect the legitimate rights and interests of creditors. It plays an important role in promoting the development of credit markets. Design/methodology/approach Based on a quasi-natural experiment of establishing bankruptcy court in China, this paper examines the impact of the establishment of bankruptcy court on shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises, using a multi-period difference-in-differences model with China's A-share listed enterprises as the research object from 2016 to 2022. Findings The findings show that the establishment of bankruptcy court increases the scale of shadow banking activities of non-financial enterprises. Furthermore, enhancing creditor protection and increasing management risk preference play important mechanism effect. Bankruptcy law enforcement efficiency demonstrates a strong moderating effect. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence for evaluating the quality and effectiveness of bankruptcy system reform and offers instructive insights for activating informal finance, regulating shadow banking activities and maintaining financial market stability.

papers.title: Political connection, earnings volatility and short-term debt
papers.abstract: Purpose Political connections introduce significant uncertainty in emerging markets and may shape firms' risk profiles by weakening market discipline and governance mechanisms. This study examines the association between political connections and earnings volatility in the Indian context. Additionally, it examines whether short-term debt can act as a moderator in mitigating the risk associated with political connections by reinforcing financial discipline and external monitoring. Design/methodology/approach Using an unbalanced panel of NSE-listed firms from 2009 to 2024, the study employs pooled ordinary least squares (OLS). The political connection is measured using a dual-channel approach, comprising both the promoter's channel and the donation channel. The political connection dataset for Indian firms was compiled from Election Commission of India contribution reports and the companies' annual reports. The results exhibit robustness to endogeneity concerns, which are addressed through instrumental variable estimation and a range of robustness tests. Findings The major findings of the study indicate that a firm with a political connection is positively and significantly associated with earnings volatility, suggesting that political connection exposes the firm to policy uncertainty, rent-seeking pressure and managerial opportunism. Short-term debt (STD) is found to reduce earnings volatility and negatively moderates the relationship between political connection and earnings volatility. This finding suggests that STD as an external governance by enhancing regular creditor monitoring. These findings align with agency theory and remain robust across alternative measures and endogeneity correction. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by providing evidence on the risk implications of political connections in an emerging market setting and by highlighting the moderating role of STD in shaping earnings volatility in politically connected firms. The findings underscore the importance of debt maturity structure as an external governance mechanism in environments characterised by political influence.

papers.title: Ex-bureaucrats and ex-politicians: impact on bank financial reporting quality
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper investigates the associations of ex-bureaucrats and ex-politicians serving on bank boards with financial reporting quality using a sample of Turkish banks over the period 2007–2022. Design/methodology/approach We mainly perform ordinary least squares and logistic regressions to test our hypothesis and address the research question. To mitigate selection bias and endogeneity problems, we perform the Heckman two-stage selection model and system GMM procedures. To mitigate the omitted variable bias, we use a fixed effects estimator. Additionally, we constructed an alternative sample by excluding ex-bureaucrats without professional experience in accounting, finance, taxation, or other relevant fields. Finally, we created interaction terms using the ex-bureaucrat and ex-politician variables. Findings The findings indicate that ex-bureaucrat directors are associated with higher financial reporting quality, particularly through lower discretionary loan loss provisions, whereas ex-politician directors exhibit no consistent association with financial reporting quality. Additional analyses provide robust support for the discretionary loan loss provision results. However, the evidence for small-profit reporting is less robust, particularly in the bank fixed-effects estimations. Furthermore, the results remain robust when ex-bureaucrats whose public sector careers were unrelated to accounting, finance, or related fields are excluded. This finding suggests that the documented association is more closely linked to the relevant expertise accumulated during bureaucratic careers than to bureaucratic status per se. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by showing that the association between ex-bureaucrats and bank financial reporting quality appears to depend on the relevant expertise accumulated during their public sector careers, rather than on bureaucratic background per se. It also offers novel evidence on the heterogeneous implications of different forms of government experience for bank financial reporting quality.

papers.title: Guest editorial: Accounting, auditing and financial management under digital governance
Analysts’ use of toxic emissions data
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether financial analysts function as information intermediaries by incorporating Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) data into their assessments of firms' environmental risks, as reflected in earnings forecasts and stock recommendations. It further investigates whether analysts' forecast and recommendation revisions influence subsequent corporate environmental performance, thereby providing evidence on the effectiveness of the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA's) market-based regulatory approach. Design/methodology/approach Using a longitudinal sample of US publicly listed firms from 1997 to 2011, the study analyzes how financial analysts utilize TRI data in their decision-making processes. An event-study methodology is employed to examine how the EPA's annual public release of TRI data affects analysts' forecast accuracy and dispersion. The analysis also examines the economic implications of analysts' forecast and recommendation revisions for firms' future toxic emissions. Robustness tests are conducted using alternative environmental risk measures and industry-level analyses. Findings The results indicate that higher pollution propensity is associated with greater forecast errors and increased dispersion among analysts. Analysts respond to increases in pollution propensity by revising earnings forecasts and stock recommendations downward, and they revise them upward when pollution propensity declines. Importantly, these analyst responses are predictive of subsequent reductions in firms' toxic emissions, suggesting that analyst activity can exert real effects on corporate environmental behavior. Overall, the findings support the role of TRI disclosures in facilitating market-based discipline. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to US firms and TRI data up to 2011. Future research could investigate other forms of noncorporate disclosure and verifiable pollution data in global contexts to enhance the generalizability of the findings. Practical implications The study provides empirical support for the EPA's use of TRI disclosures as a mechanism to encourage environmental improvements through capital-market pressure. Policymakers and standard setters may further enhance the effectiveness of such disclosures by requiring more detailed and standardized environmental information in firms' management's discussion and analysis (MD&A), thereby enabling analysts to better identify and price environmental risks. Social implications By demonstrating that financial analysts incorporate TRI disclosures in ways that can shape firms' environmental behavior, the study underscores the social importance of public transparency in holding polluters accountable. Analysts' forecast revisions and stock recommendations can trigger market responses that incentivize greater corporate eco-efficiency, resulting in lower toxic emissions and improved environmental quality, thereby benefiting affected communities and reinforcing corporate environmental responsibility. Originality/value This study offers novel evidence that financial analysts incorporate nonfinancial, noncorporate TRI data into their analyses, highlighting their role as information intermediaries in an environmental reporting context. It demonstrates that analysts are able to parse the uncertainty inherent in TRI data and translate environmental risk into financial outcomes through earnings forecast and stock recommendation revisions. Additionally, the study documents tangible effects of analyst behavior on firms' pollution abatement efforts, contributing to the literature on environmental accounting, analyst behavior and market-based regulation, with important policy implications.

papers.title: The impact of top management team regulatory focus on accounting conservatism
papers.abstract: Purpose Drawing on regulatory focus theory, this study aims to examine how top management teams' (TMTs) motivational orientations (promotion versus prevention focus) influence accounting conservatism and further explores the internal and external situational conditions that shape this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Using textual analysis to quantify TMT regulatory focus from management discussion and analysis (MD&A) across Chinese A-listed firms, this study applies multivariate regression analysis to assess the impact of regulatory focus on accounting conservatism. Findings Our results show that promotion-focused TMTs are more likely to diminish accounting conservatism, whereas prevention-focused TMTs enhance it. TMT restricted stock (internal situational factor) attenuates both the negative effect of promotion focus and the positive effect of prevention focus on accounting conservatism. Analyst coverage (external situational factor) weakens the negative effect of promotion focus on conservatism while amplifying the positive effect of prevention focus. Further subgroup analyses reveal that the effects of TMT regulatory focus are more pronounced in non-SOEs and firms with lower ownership concentration and are significantly moderated by auditor industry expertise and product-market competition, highlighting the role of internal governance and external market factors as important boundary conditions. Originality/value This study introduces TMT regulatory focus as a novel psychological determinant of accounting conservatism, shifting the literature beyond observable demographic proxies to the motivational drivers of managerial reporting behavior. Furthermore, it identifies two actionable governance levers that interact with TMT motivational orientations, offering a more nuanced framework for corporate governance and compensation design.

papers.title: The Frequency of Voluntary Disclosures and the Information Discovery Role of Analysts: A Study of Monthly Comparable Store Sales Disclosures
papers.abstract: In this study, we examine whether more frequent voluntary disclosures are associated with greater pre‐disclosure forecasting activity by analysts in the retail industry. We observe a positive association between the disclosure of monthly comparable store sales (MCSS) and the number of analysts’ quarterly sales forecasts preceding managers’ public MCSS disclosure. Moreover, we find that an increase in analysts’ pre‐disclosure forecasts correlates with heightened abnormal investor activity, including stock return volatility and trading volume, preceding the public announcement of MCSS. In addition, the magnitude of market reactions to pre‐disclosure forecasts is similar to that of reactions to post‐disclosure forecasts. The evidence suggests that when retail firms provide more frequent and timely comparable store sales (CSS) information, analysts demonstrate greater interest and research activity in providing pre‐disclosure quarterly sales forecasts. CSS is a voluntary disclosure of a key performance indicator (KPI), and the findings may be important to regulators who are considering the importance and frequency of future KPI reporting.

papers.title: Tax Policy Uncertainty and Corporate Tax Strategies
papers.abstract: This paper examines how firm‐level exposure to tax policy uncertainty affects corporate tax avoidance. Using US public firms from 2002 to 2020, we measure exposure with the tax policy risk (TPR) index of Hassan et al., which captures the share of quarterly earnings‐call discussion devoted to risks surrounding tax policy. Firms with greater exposure to tax policy uncertainty exhibit lower effective tax rates: a one‐standard‐deviation increase in TPR raises tax avoidance by 2%–3% relative to the sample mean, and the relationship survives instrumental‐variable estimation, propensity score matching, and lead‐lag tests. Consistent with real options reasoning, in which uncertainty about domestic tax policy raises the value of relocating income to less exposed jurisdictions, high‐TPR firms shift more income abroad and operate more tax‐haven subsidiaries. The response is concentrated among financially flexible firms, firms with earnings‐management expertise, and firms with market power, and shareholders value tax avoidance more highly when tax policy uncertainty is high. Our findings identify tax policy uncertainty as a distinct driver of corporate tax strategies.

papers.title: Stakeholder Orientation and Stock Investors’ Response to Earnings Reports: Evidence from Stakeholder Constituency Statutes
papers.abstract: This study examines whether stakeholder orientation, which allows directors to consider the interests of stakeholders beyond shareholders, affects investors’ responses to earnings announcements, as measured by earnings response coefficients (ERCs). We hypothesize that stakeholder orientation increases ERCs by mitigating managerial opportunism and excessive risk‐taking. Exploiting the staggered adoption of constituency statutes across U.S. states as a natural experiment, we find that stakeholder orientation increases ERCs through these channels. We further show that investors in stakeholder‐oriented firms respond more strongly to earnings news even when underlying earnings quality is held constant, suggesting that such earnings are perceived as more credible. The effect is stronger in settings with greater stakeholder conflicts, weaker monitoring, and higher consumer orientation. Overall, our findings provide evidence that stakeholder orientation enhances investor responsiveness to earnings reports by improving both the credibility and informativeness of reported earnings.

papers.title: Practitioner Perspectives: Private Equity Investment Influence on Audit Practice through Firm Leadership
papers.abstract: The accounting profession is undergoing a major shift as private equity (PE) investment accelerates and Alternative Practice Structures (APS) expand. This paper provides a qualitative snapshot of these changes through interview insights from practitioners: (1) two assurance partners at PE-backed national firms, (2) a PE investor, and (3) a strategic advisor from a firm that has declined PE funding. Seeking a short-term return on investment, PE management’s aim to rapidly increase firm value affects the audit practice through technological innovations, more audit engagements at lower costs, and the avid pursuit of non-attest services. The assurance partners laud these audit practice adaptations, whereas the PE investor cautions against only short-term priorities and the strategic advisor warns of independence concerns. The insights from these practitioners, coupled with recent regulatory actions, industry events, and relevant research, establish a foundation for PE investment effects on audit practice as well as future empirical work. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48.

papers.title: Comments of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association on Proposed International Standard on Review Engagements 2410
papers.abstract: In May 2026, the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB) issued an exposure draft revising International Standard on Auditing (ISA) 2410, Review of Interim Financial Information Performed by the Independent Auditor of the Entity’s Annual Financial Statements (IAASB 2026a). This commentary summarizes the views of the participating members of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association.

papers.title: Comments of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association on NYSE Proposed Rule Change to Amend Sections 303A.00 and 303A.07 of the NYSE Listed Company Manual (Release No. 34-106128; File No. SR-NYSE-2026-37)
papers.abstract: On August 13, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC or the Commission) published notice of a proposed rule change filed by the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE or the Exchange) that would extend, from one year to five years, the transition period within which a newly listed company must establish an internal audit function under Sections 303A.00 and 303A.07 of the NYSE Listed Company Manual (SEC 2026). This commentary summarizes the views of the participating members of the Auditing Standards Committee of the Auditing Section of the American Accounting Association. On the basis of extensive empirical literature in auditing, corporate governance, and capital markets, the Committee opposes the proposed rule change. The Exchange has failed to meet its burden of demonstrating that the proposed five-year deferral is designed to protect investors and the public interest, as required by Section 6(b)(5) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

Bridging the AI divide: local public accountants’ perceptions and structural constraints in AI readiness
papers.abstract: Purpose This research aims to explore whether an emerging “Artificial Intelligence (AI) divide” is developing in local public accounting due to disparities in professional attitudes, financial capacity, technological resources and political governance. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was employed using survey data from 172 Spanish municipalities, combined with real financial and political indicators. A linear regression model with clustered standard errors was applied to test the hypotheses. Findings Findings are consistent with an emerging AI divide in local public accounting in terms of uneven intention to use AI and institutional readiness conditions. Results indicate that public accountants are willing to assume the learning effort required to use AI when clear benefits and a legitimising environment are present. Regarding structural conditions, municipalities with stronger financial sustainability and higher economic development display greater readiness, while advanced technological resources diminish intention, potentially reflecting institutional inertia. In addition, the findings suggest that AI readiness is becoming a cross-cutting priority that depends on governments’ ability to articulate coherent strategies. Originality/value This study provides actionable value for public accountants and governments by clarifying how they can prevent an AI divide from emerging. Public accountants can assess digital readiness, advocate for training and resources and take a strategic role in leading AI-driven innovation. For local governments, it provides guidance on creating enabling conditions for AI adoption through pilots, strategic planning, financial stability and inter-municipal cooperation, while highlighting how higher-level administrations can support cohesion through shared services and capacity-building.

papers.title: Moving beyond the invisible: hidden cost accounting as a mediating device for organizational change in crisis-stricken small family-owned businesses
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how hidden cost calculations produced through the Socio-Economic Approach to Management (SEAM) mediate organizational sensemaking and professionalization in a crisis-stricken small family-owned business. Design/methodology/approach An intervention-research design using the SEAM and its Qualimetrics protocol, based on a longitudinal case study of a Lebanese industrial small family-owned business. Findings Hidden cost calculations made informal dysfunctions visible, discussable and connectable to managerial routines, functioning as mediating accounting representations rather than mechanically triggering change. Post-intervention figures are interpreted as part of the intervention record, not as causal proof of effectiveness. Research limitations/implications As a single intervention-research case, the findings are analytically rather than statistically generalizable. The hidden cost figures are negotiated estimates produced within the intervention and are not read as independent causal measurements of performance improvement. Practical implications For owner-managers, hidden cost accounting may offer a route to professionalization by translating coordination delays, rework, skill gaps and idle time into financial terms, supporting prioritization without immediate bureaucratic expansion. Social implications By making internal sources of loss visible and discussable, hidden cost accounting may help crisis-stricken firms protect productive capacity and shift from reactive cost cutting toward organizational learning. Originality/value The study contributes to interpretive management accounting and organizational change literature by showing how a socio-economic intervention can produce calculative representations through which crisis-stricken small family-owned businesses reinterpret internal dysfunctions and negotiate professionalization.

papers.title: Mapping sustainability reporting using indicator attributes
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how the attributes of reported sustainability indicators can be used to infer the reporting strategies organisations adopt. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on institutional, stakeholder and legitimacy theories, we reviewed the sustainability reporting literature to identify key reporting strategies and related indicator attributes, including reporting frequency, stakeholder focus and the direction and sensitivity of information. These attributes informed a global reporting initiative (GRI)-based coding framework, which we applied to 2,184 GRI-based sustainability reports from 364 US-listed firms in the Forbes Global 2000 between 2018 and 2023. Frequency data were analysed quantitatively, while the remaining attributes were independently coded and mapped to GRI performance indicators. Descriptive trend analysis, comparative distribution analysis and regression models were then used to examine how disclosure profiles differed across reporting groups and evolved over time. The framework was subsequently applied across the sample to identify and compare firms’ reporting strategies. Findings Indicator attributes reveal strategic differences not visible from disclosure counts alone. Firms with similar disclosure volumes may allocate reporting attention very differently across indicators, stakeholders and disclosure types, while firms with differing disclosure volumes may exhibit similar reporting profiles. The findings show that increases in disclosure volume do not necessarily correspond to broader disclosure coverage or more inclusive reporting strategies. Although reporting levels generally increased over time, disclosure profiles changed only modestly, with firms largely maintaining similar reporting orientations across the study period. A firm’s reporting approach may also appear broader under one theoretical lens but selective or concentrated under another, highlighting the importance of using multiple perspectives when assessing sustainability disclosure strategies. Originality/value The study shows the value of examining sustainability reports through multiple theoretical perspectives and introduces a structured, theory-informed approach for analysing reporting content.

papers.title: The determinants of dysfunctional audit behavior in an emerging context: a cognitive approach
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to explore the external and internal determinants of dysfunctional audit behavior in the Tunisian context using a cognitive approach. Design/methodology/approach The authors’ methodological approach is based on a cognitive approach. The authors use the cognitive mapping method to analyze 12 auditors’ cognitive maps in Tunisia. A collective map was grounded through assembling the full individual maps. Findings Using the Decision Explorer software for this analysis, the authors find that time budget pressure, client importance, turnover intention and job burnout are the most significant factors that can lead to dysfunctional audit behavior among Tunisian auditors. Practical implications This study’s findings help audit firms to identify the most significant factors that increase the probability of engaging in dysfunctional audit behavior. Furthermore, this paper contributed to the researchers, auditors and educators in further understanding of the factors that lead to dysfunctional behavior among auditors. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this research is among the first to examine internal and external factors that contribute to dysfunctional audit behavior using a cognitive approach. This paper contributes to the literature on accounting by analyzing the determinants of dysfunctional behavior based on attribution theory.

papers.title: Sustainability integration in risk assessment and management accounting: insights from Iran
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to investigate the adoption of sustainability principles by Iranian firms in their strategic planning, risk management and management accounting (MA) practices. It aims to build a structural model that demonstrates how industry-driven, sustainable risk assessment tools can enhance organizational responsibility, adaptability and adherence. Design/methodology/approach The research adopted a survey approach, serving 103 Iranian companies from different sectors of the business world. To examine these relations of strategic planning, sustainable risk assessment tools and integration of sustainability in MA systems, structural equation modeling (SEM) was used. Procedural and statistical remedies were used to check and control the common method bias. Findings The findings indicate that enterprises using sustainable risk assessment instruments are significantly more advanced with respect to the inclusion of environmental issues in MA. Environmental and social risk assessments are highly determined by strategic planning, as sustainable risk assessment tools become an important mediator between the integration of sustainability in MA and global organizational sustainability performance. Yet, there are many companies without unit-level sustainability departments or that still report sustainability within the traditional accounting systems, suggesting enduring institutional and structural impediments. Originality/value In this early empirical research in Iran, the relationship between sustainability and risk assessment and MA is explored using SEM. By embedding the sustainability integration concept in a developing economy, this study supplements the limited literature on sustainable MA in a non-Western context.

papers.title: “Less is less” or “Less is more”? Financial constraints and green innovation in a global context
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the theoretically ambiguous relationship between financial constraints and green innovation. The resource-based view holds that financial frictions impede green innovation by restricting investment in costly, risky technologies (“less is less”), whereas the induced innovation hypothesis argues that these constraints can spur creativity and adaptive problem solving, thereby enhancing green innovation (“less is more”). Design/methodology/approach This study uses the ordinary least squares (OLS) method to analyze 2,750 firms across 44 countries for the 2005–2021 period. In addition, propensity score matching, firm fixed effects, change regression and lead-dependent variable techniques are applied to address potential endogeneity concerns. Findings Results show that financial constraints reduce firms’ green innovation, supporting the “less is less” hypothesis. The effect is more pronounced among firms in countries with higher economic development, weak national governance and lax environmental policy enforcement. Reduced environmental expenditure and poor workforce wellbeing channel the effect. Institutional ownership and strong corporate governance reduce the adverse impact of financial constraints on green innovation. Practical implications This study suggests how financial constraints hinder green innovation. Specifically, the conditions under which financial constraints undermine corporate responses to climate change are clarified. Originality/value Cross-country empirical evidence of the impact of financial constraints on green innovation is scarce. This study provides valuable insights by presenting comprehensive, cross-country empirical evidence. In addition, moderation analysis offers new insights into how various factors shape the relationship between financial constraints and environmental innovation.
