papers.title: Copy, paste, and obfuscate? Readability and standardisation in integrated reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how readability and textual similarity evolve and interact in integrated reports, investigating whether narrative accessibility and textual standardisation are distinct characteristics or interconnected features of institutionalised reporting practices. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal panel of 1,393 firm-year observations from South African listed companies over 2015–2024 is analysed. Readability is measured using Flesch Reading Ease, and textual similarity using cosine similarity between consecutive reports. Fixed-effects panel regressions are supplemented by governance-excluded similarity measures, first-difference models, persistence analysis and an alternative readability measure. Findings Readability declines over time, while textual similarity remains high, with no consistent upward trend. Textual similarity is positively associated with readability, indicating that narrative continuity can coexist with greater accessibility. However, this association becomes insignificant when governance-related disclosures are excluded, suggesting that it is concentrated within a highly institutionalised disclosure domain characterised by recurring reporting requirements and stable narrative structures. Additional analyses confirm the persistence of textual similarity and robustness of the main findings. Originality/value This study extends research that has largely examined readability and textual similarity separately by demonstrating that these characteristics are interrelated and that their association depends on the disclosure domain. Greater readability can coexist with substantial textual standardisation, complicating the interpretation of this as an unambiguous indicator of disclosure quality or transparency. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing narrative accessibility, textual standardisation and substantive informativeness when evaluating corporate disclosure.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Private sustainability engagement in an emerging economy
papers.abstract: Purpose This study critically examines how private sustainability engagement functions as a form of dialogic accountability when Nordic institutional investors interact with publicly listed companies in a state-dominated emerging economy, challenging the implicit universalism of consensus-seeking engagement models. Design/methodology/approach The study employs qualitative content analysis of Nordic investor engagement reports documenting extended interactions with Egyptian financial and telecommunication companies. Legitimacy theory, neo-institutional theory and dialogic accountability provide an integrated lens for examining information exchange and corporate answerability. Findings Private engagements centre on political connections and human rights risks, with documented response patterns consistent with a prioritisation of political licence to operate over substantive answerability to international investors. The documented engagements record evidential burdens preventing independent verification. The response patterns across both cases constitute dialogic deadlock – a structural ceiling where genuine accountability exchange is foreclosed. Originality/value Empirically, the study provides an in-depth qualitative content analysis of investor-side engagement reports, documenting the sustainability information Nordic investors seek in two Egyptian private engagements and the patterns of corporate response. Theoretically, it proposes political licence and audience primacy as concepts for interpreting the documented exchanges and specifies the contextual conditions under which audience hierarchy may shift toward audience primacy. Conceptually, it theorises dialogic deadlock as a structural outcome arising where legitimacy incentives prove insufficient and the preconditions for genuine dialogic accountability are constitutively absent.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Do Big4 accounting firms affect foreign individuals’ investment decisions? Evidence from an emerging market
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper focuses on an emerging market and investigates whether a firm’s audit engagement with a Big4 accounting firm is associated with foreign individuals’ investments. We hypothesize that Big4 accounting firms’ reputation may function as a heuristic trust signal for these investors. Design/methodology/approach We tested our hypothesis by utilizing 225 non-financial firms listed on Borsa Istanbul. The dataset covers 2005 to 2023 and contains 3,590 firm-year observations. Findings Our empirical evidence indicates that foreign individuals are more likely to invest in BIST-listed firms audited by a Big4 accounting firm (AF). Our results are consistent with prior studies showing that accounting firms’ reputation is associated with investors’ decisions. Our robustness analysis suggests that Big4 AFs’ reputation may lose importance when public governance declines. Research limitations/implications The primary limitation of this research is that investor-level data are not publicly available. We also did not incorporate audit-firm-level variables such as expertise and number of partners. Practical implications Our study has implications for managers, policymakers and accounting professionals. Managers seeking to signal trust to foreign individuals may consider the positive association between Big4 AF engagement and foreign investment. Social implications Policymakers should consider measures to enhance public governance quality to attract more foreign individuals to Borsa Istanbul. Big4 AFs should note that this reputational advantage weakens as public governance declines. Originality/value While prior studies have examined institutional investors’ and mutual funds’ preferences for Big4 accounting firms, this study contributes new archival evidence on foreign individual investors’ equity investment decisions in relation to Big4 engagement in an emerging market context.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Auditors' experiences of the impact of ISA 701 on audit practice and audit accountability in South African state-owned enterprises
papers.abstract: Purpose This study explores how public sector auditors experience and interprets the implementation of International Standard on Auditing (ISA) 701, which mandates the communication of key audit matters (KAMs), with particular attention to its perceived implications for audit practice and accountability in the audit of South African State-Owned Enterprises (SOE). Design/methodology/approach The sample comprises senior external auditors and technical managers with expertise in SOE auditing in South Africa. A qualitative phenomenological approach was employed, utilising semi-structured interviews. Findings The findings suggest that auditors experienced changes in several aspects of audit practice following the implementation of ISA 701. Participants described increased technical training focused on identifying and responding to client-specific risks, as well as more structured engagement between audit leaders and audit teams in discussions of significant risks. The implementation of ISA 701 was also associated with greater involvement of technical staff, a strengthened audit review process, and an increased emphasis on professional judgement. While these changes were most evident in documentation and review practices, participants reported more limited shifts in the underlying audit approach over time as KAMs became more routine. The practice of benchmarking risk and audit procedure documentation was identified as a barrier to a client-specific, risk-based audit approach, which some participants viewed as limiting its broader implications for public accountability. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature on the application of new international auditing standards by public sector auditors and offers insight into how such standards are operationalised and mobilised to influence auditors' behaviour.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: The influence pathway of internal audit attributes on credit risk management in emerging economies: evidence from Tanzania
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how internal audit function (IAF) attributes, namely competence, independence, and leadership, influence credit risk management (CRM) in Tanzanian commercial banks, focussing on the mediating role of the IAF's sphere of influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 131 relevant employees across all 34 licenced commercial banks in Tanzania. A cross-sectional survey design was applied, and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test direct and mediated relationships. Findings Results show that IAF competence and independence significantly enhance CRM both directly and indirectly through the sphere of influence, while the relationship between leadership and CRM is fully mediated by the sphere of influence. Moreover, the sphere of influence exerts a significant positive effect on CRM, underscoring the importance of organisational influence in translating audit insights into effective risk governance. Practical implications The findings suggest that banks in emerging economies should reinforce auditor independence and competence while fostering organisational cultures that empower internal audit functions. Regulators are also encouraged to refine their supervisory frameworks to emphasise the institutional role of internal audits in risk oversight. Originality/value This study extends internal auditing research by conceptualising and validating the sphere of influence as the mechanism through which IAF attributes affect CRM. By integrating Agency Theory and Role Theory into a unified capacity–conversion framework, in which audit attributes create monitoring capacity and organisational influence converts it into governance outcomes, it offers new evidence from an emerging economy and advances understanding of how internal audit creates governance value through risk oversight in developing banking systems.

papers.journal: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
papers.title: Demand downside risk and cost structure
papers.abstract: Purpose This study investigates the impact of demand downside risk (DDR) on firms’ cost structure decisions. Drawing on Expected Utility Theory, we hypothesise that heightened DDR is associated with a less rigid cost structure, characterised by relatively lower fixed and higher variable costs. We reason that, when economic and political shocks are notably high, managers seek to avoid committed costs to limit the firm’s exposure to unfavourable demand realisations. Design/methodology/approach We used a fixed-effect model and a sample of 804 firm-year observations for manufacturing firms publicly traded on the Egyptian stock exchange between 2002 and 2019 to examine how DDR affects cost structure. Findings The empirical findings strongly confirm that firms operating in a DDR environment adopt less rigid cost structure to mitigate the high potential unfavourable demand realisations. Our results are robust to alternative model specifications. Originality/value This paper is the first of its kind to examine the cost structure of manufacturing firms in a context characterised by a high and pronounced DDR. The prior literature attempted to capture this relationship in a normal context of demand uncertainty, or a context of economic policy uncertainty (EPU), which does not reflect a high and pronounced DDR.

papers.title: Gender and respect in leadership: voices from ExCo women in the financial sector
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this article is to explore the role gender plays in the respect accorded to women leaders in the financial sector. Furthermore, the article seeks to identify ways in which disrespect is related to systemic legitimacy deficits experienced by women leaders in the sector. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a qualitative research design. Fieldwork gathered data through twenty in-depth semi-structured interviews with senior women leaders in a range of financial sector organisations. Fifteen interviews were conducted with UK leaders with remaining interviews conducted with leaders in the United States, Belgium, Brazil and The Channel Islands. Findings In a sector historically constructed as masculine terrain, findings show that women leaders in finance experience gender based (dis)respect, both overt and systemic, in ways that are related to conditional and contingent legitimacy. Women in senior leader positions are often positioned as “space invaders” to the sector. Strategic interrogation of respect and legitimacy cultures can be initiated through a systems approach. Originality/value This study frames the under-researched issue of gendered respect in leadership as a consequential construct, substantively linked to leadership legitimacy. It suggests that the notion of respect can be leveraged and embedded in the systems, structures and shared values of an organisation and can become a valuable vehicle to advance inclusion.

papers.title: Financial accountability and revenue paying behavior of citizens in local governments in Ghana: the role of trust and information technology
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the direct effect of financial accountability on citizens' revenue-paying behavior in local governments in Ghana, as well as the mediating role of trust and the moderating role of information technology in this relationship. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in stewardship theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), the study employs a quantitative survey research design and uses Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze data collected from 472 citizens across four local governments in Ghana. Findings The results show that financial accountability positively influence citizens' paying behavior of taxes and levies. Also, while information technology significantly enhances and moderate the link between financial accountability and citizen revenue paying behavior, trust is found to partially mediate this relationship. Research limitations/implications This scope of the study is limited by its reliance on self-reported data, which may result in response bias and social desirability effects. The representativeness of the sample may have been compromised as a result of the electronic survey's exclusion of individuals who did not have access to electronic media or internet. The generalisability of the study is limited by its focus on only four of the twenty-nine local governments within the research jurisdiction Practical implications The study's practical value lies in its guidance for implementing transparent financial practices, participatory governance, and digital tools to foster public trust and voluntary levies and tax compliance. Originality/value This study contributes theoretically by extending stewardship theory and UTAUT to explain revenue-paying behavior through both trust-based and technology-enabled accountability mechanisms. Methodologically, it simultaneously tests direct, mediating, and moderating effects within a single PLS-SEM framework. Contextually, the study provides evidence from Ghanaian local governments, where weak enforcement, low institutional trust, and uneven digitalization shape citizens' compliance behavior in ways that differ from developed economy settings.

papers.title: Preparers’ and auditors’ views on the accounting for development costs capitalisation: an ambiguity aversion perspective
papers.abstract: Purpose Research and development (R&D) is characterised by an ambiguous information environment where future outcomes are unknown. While archival studies document a relative prevalence of expensing development costs, this study explores the views of preparers and auditors on the accounting for the capitalisation of development costs under International Accounting Standard (IAS) 38. Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were held with 11 preparers and 10 auditors as key actors in the supply of financial reporting information. All had substantial experience in accounting for R&D. Interviewees were drawn from a range of countries reporting under International Financial Reporting Standards, which could help minimise potential bias arising from country-specific factors. An iterative interpretative thematic approach was followed for the analysis of the interview data employing ambiguity aversion. Findings Preparers and auditors portray a tendency to expensing. This finding is consistent with ambiguity aversion where individuals act as if they take a worst-case outcome and a fear of negative evaluation regarding future impairments. Moreover, this sheds light on the findings of archival studies as to a relative lack of capitalisation. Further, the findings show that the accounting treatment of development costs can be viewed as being a dialogic social construction between preparers and auditors. Practical implications This research raises important policy implications and informs the International Accounting Standards Board's (IASB) current project to comprehensively review IAS 38. Originality/value The findings advance the financial accounting literature in relation to R&D and the consideration of ambiguity and ambiguity aversion in accounting practice. Prior accounting-related studies considering ambiguity have primarily adopted an experimental design often in a training environment with students. In contrast, this research directly reports the views of highly experienced auditors and preparers regarding a key and highly topical, accounting issue.

papers.title: Converging standards, diverging outcomes? An empirical analysis of interoperability in sustainability reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This article investigates the evolving sustainability reporting landscape in the European Union (EU) following the implementation of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). It explores the degree of interoperability – that is, the effective alignment between the ESRS and major international frameworks, including the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) and the International Sustainability Reporting Standards (IFRS) – and evaluates how companies respond in practice. Design/methodology/approach The study conducts a comparative analysis of energy companies operating within the EU. The empirical analysis is supported by the construction of an interoperability grid and the subsequent measurement of interoperability indicators. Findings The analysis reveals strong alignment in disclosures between companies reporting under the ESRS and those reporting under the GRI, supporting the practical effectiveness of interoperability initiatives. In contrast, IFRS-aligned firms exhibit significantly lower and more heterogeneous disclosure levels, particularly in governance, highlighting limitations of investor-centric reporting frameworks in achieving comprehensive sustainability transparency. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on a cross-sectional sample from a single EU sector, limiting their generalisability. Nevertheless, the results inform policymakers and firms by evidencing practical interoperability between the ESRS and GRI while highlighting gaps in IFRS-aligned disclosures. Practical implications By empirically examining interoperability in practice, this study provides evidence-based insights for policymakers, standard setters, and firms, supporting alignment strategies and informing the implementation of sustainability reporting frameworks within the evolving EU regulatory landscape. Social implications Achieving a truly harmonised reporting environment across the EU would strengthen stakeholder trust, enhance the comparability of disclosures, and support effective and sustainable economic development. Originality/value This study provides empirical evidence on interoperability across the ESRS, GRI, and IFRS frameworks, offering one of the first disclosure-based assessments of cross-framework alignment in the early implementation phase of the CSRD.

papers.title: Determinants of green behaviour in the finance sector: moderating role of environmentally-specific servant leadership
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines the moderating role of Environmentally-Specific Servant Leadership (ESSL) on factors influencing green behaviour among internal stakeholders in the finance sector. The factors considered are attitude, concern, and knowledge about the environment, and perceived corporate social responsibility (CSR). Design/methodology/approach Two independent studies, involving students (n = 256) and employees (n = 233) in the financial sector, were conducted. Structural Equation Modelling was employed to test the hypothesised relationships, and a multi-group analysis was performed to compare results across the two samples. Findings The antecedents had a significant positive impact on green behaviour in both groups. ESSL was found to positively moderate the relationship between some of the antecedents and green behaviour, specifically, environmental attitude for students and perceived CSR for employees, amplifying their effect on green behaviour. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to two specific stakeholder groups within the finance sector, which may limit the generalisability of the findings to other sectors or stakeholder categories. Future research could extend this model to other industries and stakeholder groups to test the robustness of the moderating role of ESSL. Practical implications The findings have implications for policy formulation, curriculum development, and human resource strategies aimed at strengthening pro-environmental conduct among employees and future finance professionals. Originality/value The study extends the concept of respect in the finance sector beyond ethical conduct and fiduciary responsibility to environmental stewardship. By comparing the moderating effect of ESSL across two distinct internal stakeholder groups, it offers insight into how leadership shapes pro-environmental behaviour.

papers.title: Foundational perspectives on conceptual frameworks for accounting standards: advancing toward a meta-framework
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the conceptual fragmentation within the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB) Conceptual Framework (CF) by investigating the interrelationships among three fundamental accounting choices: accounting approaches (balance sheet vs. income statement), capital maintenance concepts (financial vs. physical), and measurement bases (historical cost vs. current value). It aims to develop a comprehensive meta-framework that integrates these elements through broader foundational perspectives. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a normative methodology, the study synthesizes existing theoretical debates and formalizes alternative accounting positions. Through logical analysis, it identifies consistent configurations among the three accounting choices and organizes them into three overarching foundational perspectives: market, entrepreneurial, and institutional. Findings The research demonstrates that coherent links exist among accounting approaches, capital maintenance, and measurement bases. These are structured into three foundational perspectives, each representing a distinct accounting philosophy aligned with different stakeholder needs and epistemological views. The study proposes a meta-framework that integrates these perspectives to enhance conceptual coherence and regulatory flexibility. Research limitations/implications The study is theoretical and lacks empirical validation. Further research is needed to test the applicability of the meta-framework across diverse institutional and cultural contexts and to empirically assess the role of the institutional perspective in CFs. Practical implications The framework helps standard setters, policymakers, and managers tailor accounting practices and regulations to varied stakeholder interests and organizational contexts, improving transparency and relevance in financial reporting. Originality/value The study introduces a novel meta-framework that reinterprets foundational accounting choices through integrated perspectives, offering a more pluralistic and inclusive vision for CFs.

papers.title: Preventing recurring material misstatements through behavioural sustainment: a 5S-based conceptual framework for financial reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper develops a conceptual framework to explain how behavioural discipline is sustained in routine financial reporting work and how such sustainment conditions the recurrence of material misstatements under conditions of reasonable assurance. Rather than treating reporting reliability as an outcome optimised through technical rules or ex post detection, the paper reconceptualises financial reporting as a behaviourally enacted process shaped by routines, accountability, and reinforcement over time. Design/methodology/approach The paper adopts a structured conceptual integration of accounting, management control and behavioural literature. The 5S principles – Sort, Set in Order, Shine, Standardise and Sustain – are reinterpreted as a behavioural process framework that explicates how reporting routines are enacted, coordinated, scrutinised and reinforced across reporting cycles. The approach is conceptual in nature and does not constitute a systematic review or a design science intervention. Findings The framework suggests that the recurrence of material misstatements is shaped less by the presence of additional procedures than by the extent to which disciplined reporting practices are behaviourally sustained over time. It explicates how 5S operates through behavioural mechanisms – such as selective attention to materiality, anticipatory coordination, anomaly questioning, accountable judgement and reinforcement across cycles – that condition how formal reporting requirements are enacted in practice, without assuming the elimination of judgement or error. Research limitations/implications As a conceptual paper, the framework does not provide empirical evidence of effectiveness and is developed primarily from literature grounded in regulated reporting environments. Practical implications The paper offers accountants, auditors, boards and regulators a conceptual lens for interpreting whether reporting routines are behaviourally sustained or have become symbolic, without implying a prescriptive intervention. Originality/value The paper reframes misstatement prevention as a problem of behavioural sustainment rather than technical optimisation, enabling recurring reporting failures to be analysed as manifestations of instability in routine enactment rather than isolated procedural deficiencies.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Toward resilient inter-organizational collaboration through boundary work: the perspective of frontline managers
papers.abstract: Purpose Public service organizations increasingly rely on inter-organizational collaboration to address complex societal problems that no single actor can manage alone. Public sector managers are representative for initiating and sustaining such collaboration. However, resilient inter-organizational collaboration is proven to be challenging in practice due to various forms of boundaries while previous research largely overlooks managerial boundary work from a processual view. This paper aims to enhance the understanding of developing resilient inter-organizational collaboration in public service organizations from the perspective of frontline managers who are directly involved in collaborative efforts across boundaries. Design/methodology/approach In this longitudinal qualitative single case study, we draw on participant observations of meetings and semi-structured interviews with frontline managers who represent five different caregivers in a new multi-disciplinary primary care model in a Swedish region. Our thematical analysis builds on 24 observed meetings and 10 interviews. Findings The findings show how the studied managers engage in three forms of collaborative boundary work in correspondence to three recurring boundaries in relation to administration, time and communication. The managers employ boundary work strategies in the form of managerial tactics to create a “third space”, embrace a complementary, proactive and accepting approach, and create a new “shared domain”. The tactics help to transform points of friction into points of connection and, ultimately, support the development of resilient inter-organizational collaboration. The paper contributes to research on inter-organizational collaboration by offering a processual understanding of how resilience actively unfolds through five managerial tactics in early stages of work to address common boundaries in relation to administration, time and communication. Secondly, it extends research on collaborative boundary work by illustrating how collaboration is developed through a trilogy of practices for the direct purpose of fostering collaboration in a situated inter-organizational setting with multiple boundaries and actors. Thirdly, it adds an important nuance to this theory by highlighting that collaborative boundary work practices are not inherently stable mechanisms but rather contingent upon the persistence of social conditions. Originality/value Whereas prior research often focuses on collaboration from a predominant instrumental perspective, this paper illustrates it as an unfolding process between individuals and demonstrates how resilient inter-organizational collaboration is possible to reach early on. The paper offers a novel angle on managerial boundary work in direct relation to collaboration.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Climate reporting in public sector organisations: identity construction and changes
papers.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this article is to explore climate change reporting by public sector organisations. In particular, the analysis draws attention to how public sector organisations represent themselves through climate reporting practice to construct and reproduce their identities over time. Design/methodology/approach A comprehensive content analysis of 164 annual and stand-alone sustainability reports produced by 15 public sector organisations listed on the Australian National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting register over an 11-year period from 2014 to 2024 was used for this study. The analysis is informed by Tregidga et al.'s (2014) identity framework of sustainable organisations. Findings The analysis reveals an unbalanced pattern of identity construction in public sector climate reporting, characterised by a strong focus on compliance-oriented reporting, followed by reporting on climate leadership and limited engagement with strategically “good” practices associated with legitimacy seeking. Despite evidence of more substantive climate reporting, disclosures continue to focus predominantly on metrics and statistics reflecting regulatory and policy expectations. The longitudinal analysis reinforces this identity structure, although their climate reporting has developed into a more complex communicative space through which public sector organisations simultaneously construct multiple identities over time, implying that public sector climate reporting serves as a dynamic and ongoing process of identity construction rather than a linear transition from one identity to another. The analysis across organisational types also reveals that a compliance-oriented identity is most pronounced among local governments and moderately prominent in public service organisations, whereas a leadership-oriented identity emphasising community impact and knowledge sharing is most strongly developed in public universities. Originality/value Despite the rapid development of climate reporting in corporate contexts, research on sustainability and climate reporting in the public sector is still underdeveloped, even as these organisations increasingly recognise the importance of disclosing, governing and managing climate-related impacts. This article fills the gap by exploring how disclosures on climate change have evolved over time within public sector organisations to contribute to accountability and effective policy implementation. It extends Tregidga et al.'s (2014) organisational identity framework to a public sector context, where climate reporting is characterised by the coexistence of regulatory, public value and legitimacy considerations.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Microfinance sustainability amid gender inequalities in G20 emerging economies: the role of female board representation and voice and accountability
papers.abstract: Purpose The role of microfinance institutions (MFIs) in fostering economic development in emerging markets cannot be denied. Nevertheless, concerns regarding their financial sustainability persist. This study examines the relationship between social performance and state-level governance indicators, specifically voice and accountability, in shaping the financial sustainability of MFIs. In addition, the research examines how social performance, amid prevailing gender inequalities, shapes the financial sustainability of MFIs. Design/methodology/approach We analyse panel data from MFIs across the emerging economies of the G20, sourced from the MIX Market database of the World Bank. Gender inequality index (GII) data were obtained from the United Nations Development Programme website. Using dynamic panel data analysis, specifically the generalised method of moments (GMM), we estimate robust standard errors. Additionally, we employ moderated hierarchical regression to assess the interaction effects of social performance with voice and accountability, under conditions of gender inequality. Findings The results indicate that financial sustainability in the previous period significantly predicts current performance, suggesting persistence over time. Female representation on boards enhances operational self-sufficiency (OSS), though it does not have a direct effect on return on assets (ROA). GII negatively affects both ROA and OSS. While voice and accountability (V&A) show a slightly negative association with ROA, the most compelling finding is that female board presence mitigates the adverse impacts of both GII and V&A on financial sustainability. Originality/value This study is unique in examining the combined effects of social performance and voice and accountability within the broader context of gender inequality in emerging markets.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Discretion, rotational programs and reported corruption in public procurement: an analysis of Italian municipalities
papers.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to assess whether municipalities that increased their reliance on direct award procedures (DAP) after the 2020 Italian procurement reform, which more than tripled the monetary threshold for DAP, were more likely to report corruption cases and whether staff rotation moderates this association. Design/methodology/approach The analysis focuses on Italian municipalities with more than 15,000 inhabitants over the period 2016–2023. It uses difference-in-differences and triple-difference designs to analyze, respectively, whether municipalities that increased their reliance on DAP after the reform experienced a higher likelihood of reported corruption and whether staff rotation moderated this relationship. Findings Municipalities that increased their reliance on DAP after the reform are more likely to report at least one corruption case. The results also indicate that staff rotation mitigates this association. Originality/value This paper offers novel evidence on the association between municipalities’ increased reliance on discretionary procurement procedures and reported corruption at the municipal level, complementing contract-level analyses by focusing on a nationwide regulatory change. It further extends prior experimental evidence on staff rotation by providing longitudinal, real-world evidence on how staff rotation moderates the association between increased reliance on DAPs and reported corruption when administrative discretion is increased.

papers.journal: Journal of Public Budgeting, Accounting and Financial Management
papers.title: Digital transformation and workforce resilience in social enterprises: governance for crisis readiness
papers.abstract: Purpose This study examines how digital transformation, workforce resilience and governance integration influence crisis readiness in social enterprises. It explores capability-building as a potential mechanism connecting digital transformation and governance with crisis readiness, while governance maturity and ecosystem collaboration are considered contextual conditions that may shape these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative design combined a comprehensive literature review of forty peer-reviewed studies with six semi-structured interviews involving governance, workforce and digital transformation leaders. Inductive coding identified three themes: governance for crisis readiness, digital transformation enablers and workforce resilience routines, interpreted through institutional theory and dynamic capability theory. Findings Governance embedded in digital workflows strengthens reliability and accountability. Capability-building routines such as micro-drills, peer learning, and digital literacy translate strategy into continuity outcomes. Ecosystem partnerships and institutional maturity amplify these effects by improving interoperability, resource sharing and collective learning. Practical implications Integrating governance controls within digital systems and aligning workforce development with feedback and monitoring enhances readiness, transparency and long-term sustainability. Originality/value This study develops a mechanism-informed conceptual framework that integrates governance maturity, digital transformation and workforce capability to explain potential pathways toward crisis readiness in social enterprises. It identifies capability-building as a proposed explanatory mechanism and ecosystem conditions as contextual influences, offering an integrative foundation for future empirical testing.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: The evolution of legitimacy discourse in corporate social responsibility reporting: evidence from a state-owned Irish energy company (2003-2025)
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how legitimacy is discursively constructed and stabilised over time in corporate social responsibility (CSR) reporting in a state-owned enterprise (SOE) and what these legitimacy dynamics reveal about how an SOE responds to evolving sustainable-development expectations. Design/methodology/approach The CSR sections of the Electricity Supply Board’s annual reports from 2003 to 2025 are analysed using a theory-informed computerised content analysis based on Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count categories mapped to Suchman’s (1995) legitimacy framework. To assess the mapping’s interpretive validity, the authors incorporate several robustness analyses. Findings Over the 23-year period studied, the reports increasingly and consistently used language that conveyed a sense of the ESB as a natural, accepted part of everyday life. While the report language reflected pragmatic and moral legitimacy, cognitive legitimacy was prominent. This prominence is observed across multiple analytical approaches, suggesting a stable discursive orientation. This finding suggests that in SOE contexts, legitimacy depends less on actively persuading stakeholders and more on being perceived as taken-for-granted in society. Sustainable-development transitions occur through organisations whose historically embedded societal roles can both support continuity and require continuing accountability as sustainable-development expectations change. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on a single case. Also, the operationalisation of legitimacy through linguistic proxies involves interpretive judgement. While robustness checks provide support for the findings, the results should be understood as indicative patterns, not precise measurements. Practical implications The findings highlight CSR reporting as a component of managing long-term legitimacy, particularly for publicly accountable organisations. Managers may draw on historically embedded narratives and societal connections to enhance trust and alignment with sustainable-development expectations. Social implications For policymakers and regulators, the findings suggest that sustainability reporting is more than a compliance exercise – it is part of a wider infrastructure supporting public accountability and long-term societal value, and this should inform how reporting is designed. For organisations, actively cultivating a sense of being a trusted part of society through reporting can strengthen stakeholder ties and support broader sustainable development efforts. Originality/value This study provides longitudinal evidence on the configuration of legitimacy forms in CSR reporting, showing that legitimacy dynamics in SOEs differ from prior literature and the relevance of historically accumulated legitimacy to sustainable development. It also contributes methodologically by proxying legitimacy types to automated text analysis.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Unveiling ESG ratings: corporate perspectives and institutionalisation dynamics
papers.abstract: Purpose Environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings have become a central mechanism for assessing, benchmarking and signalling corporate sustainability performance to financial investors. Yet, their widespread use persists despite ongoing criticism of their capacity to accurately reflect firms’ social and environmental contributions. This paper aims to examine this paradox from the perspective of rated companies, exploring why firms continue to engage with ESG ratings despite criticism of their effectiveness, even as investors remain their primary users. Drawing on institutional theory, the authors adopt this underexplored perspective and investigate how ESG ratings become institutionalised within organisations. Design/methodology/approach Based on abductive thematic analysis of 45 semi-structured interviews with sustainability executives from listed European firms, the authors develop a framework distinguishing between substantive and symbolic forms of ESG rating institutionalisation. Findings ESG rating adoption is shaped by institutional pressures and unfolds along a continuum. At one end, firms substantively integrate sustainability considerations into core operations; at the other, ESG ratings are used symbolically to secure external recognition and legitimacy. This study also highlights the risk of deinstitutionalisation if the limitations of ESG ratings remain unaddressed. Practical implications This study offers managers, investors and policymakers insights into navigating ESG pressures and strengthening the credibility of ESG frameworks while providing a diagnostic lens to distinguish symbolic compliance from substantive integration. Social implications While the potential deinstitutionalisation of ESG ratings could erode credibility, accountability and investor trust, substantive adoption could benefit transparency, stakeholder oversight and the diffusion of sustainability norms. Addressing their limitations is therefore crucial for maintaining credibility in the financial sector and directing capital towards companies with meaningful sustainability practices. Originality/value This study extends research on corporate responses to ESG ratings by drawing on institutional theory and developing a conceptual framework of symbolic and substantive institutionalisation from the perspective of rated companies. Specifically, it shifts the explanatory focus beyond firms’ strategic orientations by showing that corporate responses are also shaped by the institutional characteristics and structural limitations of ESG rating systems, thereby advancing the concept of ESG ratings’ deinstitutionalisation.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Board monitoring and the informational content of ESG performance
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine whether improvements in environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance are associated with subsequent realised firm outcomes and whether board monitoring conditions these relationships. Using UK FTSE 350 firms, the study evaluates whether year-on-year ESG improvements predict ESG controversies, environmental incidents, investment inefficiency and future operating performance. It further investigates whether stronger board monitoring increases the extent to which ESG improvements are associated with favourable subsequent outcomes. Design/methodology/approach The study uses an unbalanced panel of 314 FTSE 350 firms, comprising 4,396 firm-year observations from 2010 to 2024, with ESG, governance and financial data from LSEG. Panel regressions include industry and year fixed effects with firm-clustered standard errors. Board monitoring is measured using a composite index based on board independence, CEO-chair role separation and board ESG expertise. Robustness tests include disaggregated governance components, an ESG measure excluding the governance pillar, firm fixed effects, lagged specifications and multicollinearity diagnostics. Findings ESG improvements are not consistently associated with subsequent ESG controversies, investment inefficiency or future operating performance. For environmental incidents, however, the interaction between ESG improvement and board monitoring is negative and statistically significant, indicating that the association becomes more favourable as monitoring strengthens. Component-level analyses show similar negative moderation for board independence, CEO-chair separation and ESG expertise, although statistical strength varies. The result also remains when the governance pillar is excluded from the ESG measure. Lagged specifications provide more limited evidence, indicating that the relationship is outcome-specific and not persistent across all time horizons. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on UK listed firms operating within a relatively strong governance environment, which may limit generalisability to weaker institutional settings. The board monitoring index uses equal weighting, although component-level tests reduce concerns regarding this construction. The outcome measures capture specific dimensions of realised firm behaviour and do not directly measure greenwashing, managerial intent or board detection processes. Future research could examine alternative governance measures, weighting schemes, outcome intensity, other institutional settings and additional mechanisms such as ownership structure, executive incentives and external assurance. Practical implications The findings suggest that ESG score improvements should not be interpreted in isolation as evidence of substantive operational change. For boards, the results highlight the importance of effective oversight in linking ESG initiatives to underlying business practices, particularly in environmentally sensitive areas. For investors, ESG changes may be more informative when considered alongside governance characteristics. For regulators and standard setters, the evidence suggests that enhanced ESG disclosure alone may be insufficient unless supported by governance structures that promote accountability and substantive implementation. Social implications The study has broader implications for corporate accountability and stakeholder confidence in ESG information. By showing that ESG improvements are not uniformly associated with realised outcomes, the findings reinforce the need for stronger governance and scrutiny over how sustainability claims relate to actual corporate behaviour. More credible alignment between ESG performance and operational conduct may improve the usefulness of sustainability information for employees, communities, investors and other stakeholders and may help reduce the risk that symbolic improvements are interpreted as evidence of substantive social or environmental progress. Originality/value The study contributes by shifting attention from ESG levels to the informational content of ESG improvements and their association with subsequent realised outcomes. It further shows that this relationship is conditional on board monitoring and differs across outcome types. Unlike studies focused mainly on ESG disclosure or contemporaneous firm value, this study links changes in ESG performance to future adverse events, investment efficiency and operating performance. It also provides new evidence that the environmental-outcome relationship is not solely driven by the construction of the composite monitoring index or mechanical overlap with the ESG governance pillar.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Heterogeneity in organizational responses to legally mandated hybrid practices: the example of the EU Taxonomy Regulation
papers.abstract: Purpose Using the EU Taxonomy Regulation as an example, this paper aims to explore how companies respond to regulations that mandate novel hybrid practices, which combine elements of multiple institutional logics, such as environmental and financial. Design/methodology/approach Combining the institutional logics perspective and the attention-based view, the authors analyze how companies process regulatory pressures based on their internal structures and practices. This study draws on 22 semi-structured interviews across seven countries, supported by document analysis of nonfinancial reports and practitioner literature. Findings The authors find that companies allocate attention differently based on the degree of integration between environmental and financial logics in their structures. The perceived compatibility of mandated practices with existing internal structures and practices significantly influences the strategic responses adopted. Practical implications This study emphasizes that early preparedness and the internal integration of sustainability and financial practices facilitate regulatory compliance and enhance competitive positioning. Policymakers should support this through capacity-building measures to promote effective regulation adoption. Social implications The results indicate that the increase in corporate sustainability–related activities depends on the strategic response types chosen in reaction to new reporting laws, such as the EU Taxonomy. Originality/value This study adds to the understanding of heterogeneous response types when companies are confronted with novel legally mandated hybrid practices. Specifically, the authors highlight how established organizational structures and practices shape these corporate responses to new reporting practices.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Caught in ESG trap? Evidence from earnings pressure by examining CEO overconfidence and pay slice
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how firms balance long-term environmental, social and corporate governance (ESG) commitments with more tactical ESG actions aimed at managing capital-market expectations, particularly through dialogues with securities analysts. Drawing on a managerial-cognitive perspective, it investigates how CEO overconfidence and CEO pay slice shape ESG decisions under varying levels of earnings pressure. Design/methodology/approach Using a panel of 14,697 firm-year observations from S&P 1500 firms over 2003–2024, the study estimates OLS regressions of tactical ESG investing on earnings pressure and its interactions with CEO overconfidence and pay slice, and applies time-series clustering to firms’ ESG score trajectories to identify distinct behavioral patterns and industry-driven groupings. Findings The analysis finds that overconfident CEOs are more likely to pursue long-term ESG strategies and resist short-term tactical ESG responses under earnings pressure. In contrast, a high CEO pay slice is associated with increased tactical ESG engagement to meet analyst expectations. Time series clustering reveals industry-driven ESG behavior patterns, reinforcing the need to align governance mechanisms with executive traits and contextual factors in ESG strategy formulation. Practical implications Sustainable development cannot be advanced merely by increasing the visibility or quantity of ESG activity; governance systems must protect the time horizon, substance and accountability of sustainability commitments. Boards and sustainability committees, compensation committees, investors and regulators should therefore reward durable, outcome-oriented ESG implementation over easily adjustable actions that mainly relieve short-term market pressure. Social implications By distinguishing tactical from strategic ESG engagement, the study shows how short-term capital-market pressure may weaken the durability and substance of the corporate sustainability commitments − the sustained investments in capabilities, stakeholder relationships and environmental and social practices − on which social resilience, environmental protection and accountable governance ultimately depend. Originality/value This study reconceptualizes CEO overconfidence as a context-dependent moderator of ESG responses to earnings pressure rather than a simple driver of ESG scores, identifies CEO pay slice as a temporal incentive mechanism and introduces shape-based time-series clustering to uncover the structure of ESG evolution for sustainable development.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Small caps, large climate data gaps: disclosure shortfalls and investment implications amid regulation retreats
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to establish small-cap investment relevance, examine portfolio risk exposures of small-cap stocks screened by environmental data availability, and explore disclosure coverage under three Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) threshold specifications. Design/methodology/approach This study analyses MSCI index returns during 2001–2025 and 2023 Scope 1–3 emissions data availability for 7,895 constituents. We constructs value-weighted portfolios of disclosed and non-disclosed small-cap firms, estimates risk exposure differences using Fama–French six-factor models, and compares climate–data coverage across three CSRD threshold specifications. Findings Small-cap indices recorded higher returns and risk-adjusted performance than mid + large-cap peers, though firm size is not a causal driver. Emissions coverage is lower among small caps, especially for Scope 3 and in Emerging Markets. Non-disclosed-minus-disclosed small-cap portfolios have positive monthly alphas of 1.0–1.5 percentage points and exhibit systematic differences in growth, momentum and, in Developed Markets, profitability exposures. These estimates reflect portfolio-selection effects rather than a causal disclosure effect and may capture omitted firm characteristics or model specification. Applying the original CSRD (the relaxed Omnibus) thresholds leaves 0%–4% (48.5%) of small-cap (Emerging Markets small-cap Scope 3) market value outside the reporting perimeter. Practical implications Climate-conscious investors using climate-data disclosure-based screens may take unintended factor positions when seeking market exposure or benchmark tracking. Lower reporting thresholds expand small-cap coverage, while wider exemptions preserve climate–data gaps. This study’s findings relate to climate accountability (SDG 13) and international disclosure coordination (SDG 17), but not to effects on financing, employment or inequality. Originality/value The study integrates small-cap performance, climate–data availability, portfolio screening and regulatory coverage.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Cultivating strength inside and out: green credit interest subsidy policies and corporate energy efficiency – new evidence from China
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the effect of green credit interest subsidy policies on corporate energy efficiency, examine their potential complementarity with government environmental regulation and explore the internal capability-building channels that may underlie firms’ responses to the coordination of fiscal and financial policies. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data on Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2022, this study employs a machine learning-enhanced difference-in-differences approach to estimate the effect of exposure to green credit interest subsidy policies on corporate energy efficiency. It further conducts policy-interaction, potential-channel and heterogeneity analyses to examine possible policy complementarities, firms’ internal responses and differences in the estimated policy effect across firms. A series of robustness checks is also performed to assess the sensitivity of the main findings. Findings The findings indicate that exposure to green credit interest subsidy policies is associated with a significant improvement in corporate energy efficiency. The estimated interaction terms provide evidence of potential complementarity between these policies and both government administrative environmental penalties and R&D subsidies. Formal coefficient-difference tests suggest that the estimated complementarity is stronger for administrative environmental penalties than for R&D subsidies. The potential-channel analysis further shows that policy exposure is associated with a lower text-based measure of potential greenwashing risk, greater green technological innovation and higher environmental investment. These findings are consistent with, but do not causally establish, the proposed internal capability-building channels. Formal between-group tests also indicate that the estimated policy effect differs significantly according to regional manufacturing agglomeration, environmental information transparency, corporate cash holdings and firm size. Research limitations/implications This study relies primarily on publicly available data from Chinese A-share listed firms, thereby precluding a full examination of corporate micro-level decision-making processes and policy implementation nuances. Future research could thus integrate survey-based evidence with quantitative approaches to investigate industry-specific policy effects. Furthermore, examining the trade-offs between policy incentives and regulatory enforcement in promoting corporate sustainable transformation represents a promising avenue for subsequent inquiry. Practical implications The findings provide practical guidance for policymakers seeking to improve corporate energy efficiency through coordinated fiscal and financial policies. Strengthening the coordination between green credit interest subsidy policies and environmental regulation can more effectively enhance firms’ internal green capabilities (i.e. the firm-level technical and managerial competencies required for green innovation), thereby stimulating green technological innovation and ultimately accelerating corporate green transformation. Social implications By improving corporate energy efficiency and promoting green transformation, green credit interest subsidy policies contribute to resource conservation, carbon emission reduction and the achievement of sustainable development goals. The findings also provide policy evidence for fostering environmentally responsible corporate behavior and supporting China’s carbon peaking and carbon neutrality objectives. Originality/value This study contributes to the sustainability accounting, green finance and environmental policy literature by providing new firm-level evidence on the relationship between regional green credit interest subsidy policies and corporate energy efficiency. It also provides evidence consistent with several potential internal capability-building channels and highlights the possible complementary role of environmental regulation in strengthening the estimated policy effect.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Heterogeneous stock market reactions to a sustainability reporting mandate: insights from the European Union
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how capital markets respond to the implementation of the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS). Both instruments are key components of the European Green Deal, designed to provide the standardized sustainability information needed to channel capital toward sustainable activities and strengthen corporate accountability. Design/methodology/approach The authors conduct an event study on five regulatory milestones – three CSRD-related and two ESRS-related events – using a matched sample of EU- and US-listed firms. In cross-sectional analyses, the authors further examine the moderating role of voluntary disclosure and environmental performance. Findings The event study results reveal heterogeneous stock market reactions. Reactions to CSRD events are significantly negative, indicating that investors view the new mandate as a cost burden. In contrast, ESRS-related events elicit positive reactions, suggesting that investors value the expected improvements in standardization and information quality. In addition, the cross-sectional analysis shows that voluntary sustainability reporting mitigates negative reactions to CSRD events, while strong environmental performance is associated with more favorable reactions to ESRS events. Research limitations/implications The findings provide new evidence of the impact of sustainability reporting mandates on financial market dynamics by disentangling investor reactions to the mandate (CSRD) and its more detailed standards (ESRS). Future work should examine postimplementation effects and cross-country variation in enforcement within the EU. Practical implications Policymakers and firms can use these insights to improve the design and communication of sustainability reporting initiatives and to anticipate investor responses. The findings directly relate to the simplification debate that culminated in the revised CSRD (Directive (EU) 2026/470) and the simplified ESRS, highlighting that these reforms should preserve the standardization benefits investors valued in our setting. Social implications The findings show that capital markets value standardized sustainability information, indicating that appropriately designed disclosure mandates can support the financing of the sustainable transition and the societal monitoring of corporate impacts. Originality/value This study offers novel evidence separating investor responses to regulatory mandates (CSRD) and standardization instruments (ESRS), highlighting the market relevance of disclosure regulation design.

papers.journal: Sustainability Accounting, Management and Policy Journal
papers.title: Exploring the role of intellectual capital in EU taxonomy compliance: the mediating effect of sustainability reporting
papers.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate whether intellectual capital (IC) can support firms in meeting the EU Taxonomy for Sustainable Activities reporting requirements. Building on resource-based view and resource orchestration theory, it examines whether mature, business-integrated sustainability reporting acts as an orchestration mechanism that transforms IC into a strategic lever for regulatory compliance and competitive advantage. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a fixed-effects model applied to a panel of large European firms that reported KPIs relating to the EU Taxonomy over the period 2018–2024. A mediation framework is applied to examine both the direct and indirect effects of IC and its components (human, structural and relational capital) on the ability to meet the disclosure requirements imposed by the Taxonomy. To address potential endogeneity issues and capture temporal dynamics, the analysis also employs the generalized method of moments (GMM) and a dynamic lagged-variables model. Furthermore, a moderated mediation model is developed to test whether the assurance of sustainability reports by a Big 4 firm moderates the strength of the mediation effect. Findings The results suggest that IC exerts a significant impact on the EU Taxonomy compliance through the mechanism of structured sustainability reporting systems. A detailed analysis of the individual components indicates that human capital exerts a positive indirect effect, whilst relational capital appears to act primarily as a direct driver. Conversely, structural capital does not show a statistically significant effect in most specifications. These results indicate that IC alone does not necessarily guarantee superior compliance capacity. Instead, its effectiveness depends on managerial coordination mechanisms. Mature sustainability reporting systems can translate intangible capabilities into standardized and transparent disclosures, in line with regulatory expectations, particularly in data-intensive contexts such as the EU Taxonomy. The findings carry significant implications for both sustainability policy development and managerial practice. Practical implications The study offers valuable insights for companies seeking to leverage their internal capabilities to meet new regulatory requirements, highlighting the role of reporting maturity as a key enabler of sustainable performance and long-term sustainable development. It also provides policy-relevant indications by emphasizing the importance of fostering organizational practices that enhance the effective use of IC within structured reporting systems. Social implications This study contributes to a deeper understanding of how intangible resources, when effectively integrated into mature sustainability reporting processes, can support firms in aligning with evolving sustainability policy frameworks by linking the management of intangible assets to measurable environmental outcomes, as defined by the EU Taxonomy framework. These findings also generate important policy implications for regulators and policymakers, who should recognize that a company’s ability to adapt depends not only on its size, but also on how its underlying intangible resources are structured and on the presence of robust reporting infrastructures capable of supporting sustainable development objectives. Originality/value Despite the growing interest in the EU Taxonomy, the firm’s internal determinants related to the new regulatory requirements remain unexplored. Therefore, this study aims to fill this gap by exploring the interplay between IC, sustainability reporting and EU Taxonomy compliance. Findings suggest a new theoretical perspective whereby IC is not a direct antecedent of sustainability, but rather a set of potential resources that require organizational capabilities to be effectively mobilized and to produce advantage.

papers.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
papers.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

papers.title: Unintended Consequences of Holding Dollar Assets
papers.abstract: We propose and examine a novel mechanism whereby holdings of dollar assets by foreign institutions can have a large, unexpected impact on foreign Treasury yields in crisis periods. Non‐U.S. institutions hold substantial dollar assets and hedge dollar exposures by selling dollars forward. In crisis periods, the dollar appreciates against other currencies. To meet margin calls on foreign exchange (FX) hedging positions, traditionally passive institutions liquidate domestic safe assets to raise cash. We show that during the recent COVID crisis, U.K. institutions with substantial dollar holdings and FX hedging positions sold large amounts of gilts, contributing significantly to the observed gilt yield spike.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
papers.abstract: We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

papers.title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
papers.abstract: Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

papers.title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
papers.abstract: We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral ) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

papers.title: Externalities of Responsible Investments
papers.abstract: We develop a model to study the efficiency of socially responsible investing (SRI) as a mechanism to control firms' externalities. When SRI is not too popular, responsible investors favor strategies that lead to a concentration of SRI in a subset of firms in the economy. This concentration can mitigate coordination issues in adopting green technologies, but it can also crowd out the green investments of excluded firms and increase the price of green products. In equilibrium, responsible investors continue to favor concentration even as SRI becomes more popular, and concentrate the most when concentration is least desirable.

papers.title: Risk, Specialization, and Covered‐Interest Parity
papers.abstract: Prevailing theories of financial intermediation assume an integrated financial sector with frictionless risk‐sharing. However, we identify substantial risk‐sharing frictions linked to intermediary specialization using currency derivatives markets as a laboratory. Using confidential supervisory data covering $25 trillion in daily bank exposures, we document imperfect hedging in banks' FX‐swap intermediation: banks rarely hedge their synthetic dollar lending with maturity‐matched foreign safe assets. Intermediaries specialize in markets in which they have expertise in managing the associated exposures, giving rise to cross‐market variation in deviations from covered‐interest parity. Our results highlight the importance of intermediary specialization and its impact on risk premia.
